A Burgers-vortex closure for the dissipative scales of turbulence: evidence, model selection and use in CFD

Working paper (Burgers Vortex Energy Balance). Symbols: \(\gamma\) axial stretching rate, \(\Gamma\) circulation, \(\nu\) kinematic viscosity, \(\varepsilon\) dissipation rate per unit mass, \(\eta\), \(U_\eta\), \(\gamma_\eta\) the Kolmogorov length, velocity and rate, \(Re_\lambda\) the Taylor-scale Reynolds number, \(r_{\max}=\beta\eta\) the radius of maximum swirl of a tube and \(U_{\max}\) that swirl.

Abstract

The smallest scales of turbulence, where micromixing and viscous dissipation take place, are organised in stretched vortex tubes. We model a tube as a Burgers vortex, close its energy budget with the Kolmogorov scales, and determine its two free quantities, the radius of maximum swirl and the swirl velocity, from 18 published sources (simulations and experiments) covering \(35\le Re_\lambda\le1934\). Every number is traced from the page of its paper to the fit in an open recording book, and each correction is listed with its rationale. The radius is \(r_{\max}\approx5\,\eta\) in all flows (5.2 \(\eta\) fitted); simulations and experiments together show only a very small reduction with the Reynolds number, from 5.3 \(\eta\) at \(Re_\lambda=100\) to 4.5 \(\eta\) at 2000. With the corrections adopted for probe measurements, a single one-parameter law, \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=0.834\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}\), predicts sources left out of the fit to within 12.3%, and no model with more parameters predicts them better. A review of the sources shows, however, that the uncorrected data separate into two populations: the 1% most intense tubes, \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=1.29\,Re_\lambda^{0.32}\), and all tubes, \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=2.00\,Re_\lambda^{0.13}\). The second reading needs one fitted probe factor instead of two corrections and reproduces the measured volume fraction of the tubes. We give the closure in a form usable in computational fluid dynamics, with the tube strain rate, circulation, volume fraction and spacing as functions of the local \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\), and add a first-order lag for the time the energy cascade takes to reach the tubes, \(T_c/\tau_\eta=C_c\,(Re_\lambda/\sqrt{15}-\beta^{2/3})\).

Keywords: micromixing; vortex tubes; Burgers vortex; turbulence closure; energy cascade; model selection.

1. Introduction

Fast reactions, precipitation and the break-up of drops are controlled by the motion at the dissipative scales of turbulence. Engineering models of micromixing picture that motion as stretched vortices of about ten Kolmogorov lengths that engulf fluid at a rate set by \((\varepsilon/\nu)^{1/2}\) (Bałdyga and Bourne 1984, 1989). Direct numerical simulations have since shown such vortices directly: the intense vorticity of isotropic turbulence is concentrated in tubes with a radius of four to five \(\eta\) (Jiménez et al. 1993; Ghira et al. 2022), and tubes with a similar radius are found in mixing layers, channels and jets (Tanahashi et al. 2001, 2004; Da Silva et al. 2011) and in hot-wire records up to \(Re_\lambda\approx2000\) (Belin et al. 1996; Mouri et al. 2007; Mouri and Hori 2009). The profile of a tube is close to that of the Burgers (1948) vortex, a balance of axial stretching and radial diffusion.

A closure for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) needs more than the picture: it needs the size, the swirl, the strain rate and the number of the tubes as functions of quantities the flow solver has. This paper derives those functions. The Burgers vortex has two free quantities, the stretching rate \(\gamma\) and the circulation \(\Gamma\). The radius of maximum swirl fixes the first, the swirl velocity the second, and an energy balance of tube and background (sections 3–7) then gives the volume fraction and the spacing of the tubes without a further constant. The radius and the swirl have to come from data, and three difficulties arise. The papers define the radius and the velocity of a tube in different ways. Probe measurements see a tube along a chord and need a correction. And the papers select different tubes: the 1% of the volume with the highest vorticity, the events above a threshold, or all tubes.

The contribution of this paper is fourfold. (i) All data are taken from the papers by a documented path: a recording book (LIT/record, one tab a paper) shows the page of the paper, the number read from it, each conversion, each assumption and the value that enters the fit (section 9). (ii) The model is chosen with an explicit penalty on complexity, by leaving each source out in turn (section 10). (iii) The review of the sources shows that the corrections adopted for the swirl are not needed if intense tubes and all tubes are treated as two populations; this second reading is developed in section 12 next to the single law of section 11, so that the reader can judge both. (iv) The closure is written for use in CFD, and the time the cascade needs to bring energy to the tubes is added as a lag (section 13). Sections 2 to 8 give the theory.

2. Theory background

Vortex stretching

In an incompressible flow the vorticity \(\boldsymbol\omega=\nabla\times\mathbf u\) follows

$$\frac{D\boldsymbol\omega}{Dt}=(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\nabla)\mathbf u+\nu\nabla^2\boldsymbol\omega .$$

The first term on the right is vortex stretching: a strain rate \(\gamma\) along the vorticity raises \(|\boldsymbol\omega|\) at the rate \(\gamma\) and, because the circulation is conserved (Kelvin), thins the vortex. The last term is viscous diffusion, which spreads the vorticity at the rate \(\nu/r^2\). Small scales are made by stretching and removed by viscosity; in turbulence the vorticity lies preferentially along the intermediate eigenvector of the strain, which is mostly extensional (Ashurst et al. 1987), so the stretching is persistent.

The Burgers vortex

Burgers (1948) found the exact steady solution in which the two effects balance: a vortex of circulation \(\Gamma\) in the axisymmetric strain \(\mathbf u=(-\gamma r/2,\,0,\,\gamma z)\), whose radial inflow convects the vorticity inwards as fast as viscosity spreads it out,

$$u_\theta=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\left(1-e^{-\gamma r^2/4\nu}\right),\qquad \omega_z=\frac{\Gamma\gamma}{4\pi\nu}\,e^{-\gamma r^2/4\nu}.$$

Its size, \(r_{\max}=2.24\sqrt{\nu/\gamma}\) (section 3), depends on the strain and the viscosity and not on the circulation; its Reynolds numbers are \(Re_\gamma=\gamma r_{\max}^2/\nu=4x=5.03\) (fixed) and \(Re_c=r_{\max}U_{\max}/\nu\) or \(\Gamma/\nu=8.78\,Re_c\) (free). The dissipation it adds to the strain, \(\rho\gamma\Gamma^2/8\pi\) per unit length, does not depend on \(\nu\) (section 3). The vortex is a model: the strain is imposed and does not feel the vortex.

Stretched vortices in turbulence

Townsend (1951) described the fine structure of turbulence as a collection of Burgers-type vortex sheets and tubes. Tennekes (1968) built the small scales from a random array of Burgers vortices and derived their spectrum and size. Lundgren (1982) wound a vortex sheet into a spiral round a stretched tube (the strained spiral vortex), which gives the \(k^{-5/3}\) spectrum, and Horiuti and Fujisawa (2008) extended the idea to several modes in a simulation. Robinson and Saffman (1984) and Neu (1984) studied how a stretched vortex is changed by a non-axisymmetric strain and by its own induced flow. Moffatt, Kida and Ohkitani (1994) showed for large Reynolds number \(\Gamma/\nu\) that the stretched vortex is an asymptotic solution of the Navier–Stokes equations when the strain is not axisymmetric, called such vortices the sinews of turbulence, and found that the excess dissipation of a Burgers vortex does not change in a non-axisymmetric strain while 98.7% of it falls outside \(r=\sqrt2\,\delta\), where only 37% of the enstrophy sits (section 3). The tube is thus the part of the structure that carries the vorticity, and most of the dissipation it causes lies in its shear layer.

Scales and what the Burgers vortex says about them

Richardson (1922) pictured the energy passing from large eddies to smaller ones, and Kolmogorov (1941) gave the scales at which it ends, set by \(\nu\) and the dissipation \(\varepsilon\):

$$\eta=\left(\frac{\nu^3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/4},\qquad U_\eta=(\nu\varepsilon)^{1/4},\qquad \gamma_\eta=\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\nu}\right)^{1/2},\qquad Re_\eta=\frac{U_\eta\eta}{\nu}=1 .$$

Dissipation is intermittent (Meneveau and Sreenivasan 1991) and the velocity-gradient field is organised in vortex tubes and sheets (Nomura and Post 1998). Write the Burgers vortex in Kolmogorov units, \(r_{\max}=\beta\eta\) and \(U_{\max}=u\,U_\eta\). Then \(\gamma r_{\max}^2=4x\nu\) gives

$$\beta^2\,\frac{\gamma}{\gamma_\eta}=4x=5.03,\qquad Re_c=\beta\,u,\qquad \frac{\Gamma}{\nu}=8.78\,\beta u .$$

By dimensional analysis the two numbers \(\beta\) and \(u\) depend on \(Re_\lambda\) only, and nothing else about the tube is free. This is what sections 9–11 determine from the data. A radius of \(5\eta\) means a strain \(\gamma=0.2\,\gamma_\eta\): the strain that stretches the tubes is a fixed fraction of the Kolmogorov strain at every \(Re_\lambda\). One reading is that where the strain exceeds the Kolmogorov value eddies form and reduce it, so that the strain that survives around a tube is a fraction of \(\gamma_\eta\); the radius and the strain are then one observation, not two.

Simulations and experiments

The tubes were found in simulations as connected regions of high vorticity, the worms of Jiménez et al. (1993) and Jiménez and Wray (1998), and later as the intense vorticity structures (the 1% of the volume of highest vorticity) whose radius is the 1/e radius of the vorticity (Da Silva et al. 2011; Ghira et al. 2022, 2025; Moisy and Jiménez 2004 on their geometry and clustering). Other definitions give more of the volume: low-pressure vortex cores (Kida et al. 2002; Makihara et al. 2002; 31–35% of the volume), coherent fine-scale eddies from the second invariant of the velocity gradient (Tanahashi et al. 2001, 2004), cores scanned out of a database without a threshold (Pirozzoli 2009, 2012) and vortex tubes in thin shear layers (Ishihara et al. 2011, 2013; Elsinga et al. 2023). In experiments a tube is a conditional average of the signal around events of a large velocity increment, fitted with a Burgers profile (Mouri et al. 2003, 2004, 2007; Mouri and Hori 2009; Sassa and Makita 2005), or the tails of the distribution of a velocity derivative (Belin et al. 1996), or an objectively defined vortex in a 3D measurement (Aligolzadeh et al. 2023). The radius is about 5 \(\eta\) in all of them once the geometry of the cut and the definition are accounted for (section 9); the swirl and the circulation differ because the selection decides which tubes are counted (section 9).

3. One stretched vortex

Velocity profile and core size

With viscous core length \(\delta=\sqrt{\nu/\gamma}\), the azimuthal velocity is

$$U_\theta(R)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi R}\left(1-e^{-\gamma R^2/4\nu}\right).$$

Put \(x=\gamma R^2/4\nu\). The velocity peaks where

$$e^{x}-2x-1=0\;\Rightarrow\;x=1.2564,\qquad r_{\max}=\sqrt{4x}\,\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\gamma}}=2.242\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\gamma}}.$$ $$U_{\max}=\frac{1-e^{-x}}{2\pi}\,\frac{\Gamma}{r_{\max}}=0.1138\,\frac{\Gamma}{r_{\max}}=0.0508\,\Gamma\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{\nu}},\qquad \Gamma=8.78\,U_{\max}\,r_{\max}.$$

Dissipation of the whole structure

The background strain is irrotational, so integrating the enstrophy isolates the excess caused by the vortex (Burgers eq. 60, Moffatt eq. 3.36):

$$P_{\text{ex}}=\rho\nu\int_0^\infty \omega^2\,2\pi r\,dr=\frac{\rho A C^2}{4\pi}=\frac{\rho\,\gamma\,\Gamma^2}{8\pi}\quad\text{per unit length.}$$

It does not depend on \(\nu\). Moffatt's addition is that non-axisymmetric strain leaves this total unchanged while 98.7% of it falls outside \(r=\sqrt2\,\delta\), where only 37% of the enstrophy sits.

4. Dissipation as flow times pressure drop

The radial inflow through the cylinder \(r=r_{\max}\), per unit length, uses \(\alpha+\beta=-\gamma\):

$$Q=\pi r_{\max}^2\,\gamma .$$

Dividing the dissipation by \(Q\) cancels \(\gamma\):

$$\frac{P_{\text{ex}}}{Q}=\frac{\rho\,\Gamma^2}{8\pi^2 r_{\max}^2}=\frac{\rho\,U_{\max}^2}{2\,(1-e^{-x})^2}=0.977\,\rho\,U_{\max}^2=1.954\cdot\tfrac12\rho U_{\max}^2 .$$

\(P_{\text{ex}}=Q\,\Delta P\) with \(\Delta P\approx\rho U_{\max}^2\), matching the core pressure drop Burgers quotes. The same constant holds for Moffatt's non-axisymmetric strain.

There is no excess axial velocity: the vortex induces only cross-flow motion and \(U_z=\gamma z\) is the background. The "axial energy flux" branch in the session (constants 3.73, 0.244, 0.593, 0.379) was withdrawn by Gemini and should be dropped.

5. Background strain dissipation

For \(U=(\alpha x,\beta y,\gamma z)\) with \(\alpha=-\tfrac12(1+\lambda)\gamma\), \(\beta=-\tfrac12(1-\lambda)\gamma\):

$$\varepsilon_{\text{strain}}=2\nu\left(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\right)=\nu\gamma^2\left(\lambda^2+3\right)\;\xrightarrow{\;\lambda=0\;}\;3\nu\gamma^2 .$$

6. Global budget

\(Q\) is per metre of vortex (m²/s) and \(L_e\) is the vortex length per unit volume (m/m³), so \(L_eQ\) is the volume drawn into the cores per second per unit volume, in 1/s. The budget fixes it:

$$\varepsilon-3\nu\gamma^2=0.977\,(L_eQ)\,U_{\max}^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad L_eQ=\frac{\varepsilon-3\nu\gamma^2}{0.977\,U_{\max}^2}.$$

The core volume fraction is then an output, not an input. Derivation: each metre of tube occupies the cross-section \(\pi r_{\max}^2\) (m³ per m of tube), and there are \(L_e\) metres of tube per m³ of fluid, so the fraction of volume inside the cores is

$$V_f=L_e\,\pi r_{\max}^2 .$$

The inflow per metre of tube is \(Q=\pi\gamma r_{\max}^2\) (section 4), so \(\pi r_{\max}^2=Q/\gamma\) and

$$V_f=\frac{L_eQ}{\gamma}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_eQ=V_f\,\gamma .$$

Meaning: the cores hold a fraction \(V_f\) of the volume, and the strain field refills that volume at the rate \(\gamma\), so the volume drawn in per second per unit volume is \(V_f\gamma\). Because \(V_f\) is a fraction of the cylinder's own cross-section, it is a cross-section of the core, not of the whole dissipative eddy. The dissipation spreads over a larger radius than \(r_{\max}\) (98.7% of it lies outside \(r=\sqrt2\,\delta\)); that is a limit of this \(Q\,\Delta P\) bookkeeping.

Correction to the session. Gemini assumed \(V_f=1\%\) as an input and reduced \(L_eQ\) to \(0.0503\,\nu\). That value has units m²/s, because it cancelled \(\pi r_{\max}^2\) against a \(Q\) already evaluated as \(5.03\,\nu\) (which also dropped a factor \(\pi\)). It then discarded the mismatched term as "negligible". The 22.8% eddy share it reported came from that slip. With the units kept, \(L_eQ=V_f\gamma\) and everything is consistent.

7. Closing with Kolmogorov scales

$$\eta=\left(\frac{\nu^3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/4},\quad U_\eta=(\nu\varepsilon)^{1/4},\quad \gamma_\eta=\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\nu}},\quad U_\eta\,\eta=\nu .$$

Assumption: the tube's peak-swirl radius and peak velocity scale with the Kolmogorov scales through one dial \(\beta\),

$$r_{\max}=\beta\,\eta,\qquad U_{\max}=\beta\,U_\eta .$$

Fixing the two separately would overdetermine the problem, which caused the repeated loops in the session. Here \(\beta\) is just \(r_{\max}/\eta\), the tube radius in Kolmogorov lengths (the core diameter is \(2\beta\eta\)).

Step 1: what \(x\) is and where it comes from

\(x\) is the dimensionless radius squared of the Burgers vortex,

$$x(R)=\frac{\gamma R^2}{4\nu}=\left(\frac{R}{2\delta}\right)^2,\qquad \delta=\sqrt{\nu/\gamma}.$$

Substituting \(R^2=4\nu x/\gamma\) into \(U_\theta=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi R}\left(1-e^{-x}\right)\) gives the velocity as a function of \(x\) alone:

$$U_\theta=\frac{\Gamma}{4\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{\nu}}\;\frac{1-e^{-x}}{\sqrt{x}} .$$

The peak is where \(\mathrm d/\mathrm dx\left[(1-e^{-x})\,x^{-1/2}\right]=0\):

$$e^{-x}x^{-1/2}-\tfrac12(1-e^{-x})x^{-3/2}=0\;\Rightarrow\;2x\,e^{-x}=1-e^{-x}\;\Rightarrow\;e^{x}-2x-1=0 .$$

This has the single positive root (found by Newton iteration) $$\boxed{\,x=1.25643\,},\qquad e^{x}=3.51286=2x+1,\qquad 1-e^{-x}=0.71533 .$$ So \(x\) is a pure number fixed by the shape of the profile. It converts between the peak radius and the viscous scale:

$$r_{\max}^2=\frac{4x\,\nu}{\gamma}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma=\frac{4x\,\nu}{r_{\max}^2}.$$

Step 2: strain rate from \(r_{\max}=\beta\eta\)

The Kolmogorov scales satisfy \(\eta^2=\nu/\gamma_\eta\) with \(\gamma_\eta=\sqrt{\varepsilon/\nu}\). Then \(r_{\max}^2=\beta^2\nu/\gamma_\eta\), and

$$\gamma=\frac{4x\,\nu}{\beta^2\nu/\gamma_\eta}=\frac{4x}{\beta^2}\,\gamma_\eta .$$

Step 3: circulation from \(U_{\max}=\beta U_\eta\)

The peak velocity in terms of \(\Gamma\) and \(r_{\max}\) is \(U_{\max}=\frac{(1-e^{-x})\,\Gamma}{2\pi r_{\max}}\). Solving for \(\Gamma\) and inserting both conditions together with \(U_\eta\eta=\nu\):

$$\Gamma=\frac{2\pi\,r_{\max}U_{\max}}{1-e^{-x}}=\frac{2\pi\,(\beta\eta)(\beta U_\eta)}{1-e^{-x}}=\frac{2\pi}{1-e^{-x}}\,\beta^2\,\nu=8.78\,\beta^2\,\nu .$$

Step 4: the Reynolds numbers

Three Reynolds numbers appear. Each is a velocity times a length over \(\nu\).

NameDefinitionValue with \(r_{\max}=\beta\eta,\ U_{\max}=\beta U_\eta\)
Circulation Re, \(R_\Gamma\)\(\Gamma/\nu\)\(8.78\,\beta^2\)
Core Re, \(Re_c\)\(U_{\max}r_{\max}/\nu\)\(\beta^2\)
Strain Re, \(Re_\gamma\)\(\gamma r_{\max}^2/\nu\)\(4x=5.03\)

\(R_\Gamma\) is the inverse of Moffatt's small parameter, \(\epsilon=\nu/\Gamma=1/R_\Gamma\), so the asymptotic theory needs \(R_\Gamma\gg1\). The core Reynolds number follows from the \(U_{\max}\) relation above:

$$Re_c=\frac{U_{\max}r_{\max}}{\nu}=\frac{\beta U_\eta\cdot\beta\eta}{\nu}=\beta^2,\qquad R_\Gamma=\frac{2\pi}{1-e^{-x}}\,Re_c=8.78\,Re_c=8.78\,\beta^2 .$$

The strain Reynolds number is just Step 1 rearranged, so it is the same for every Burgers vortex: \(Re_\gamma=\gamma r_{\max}^2/\nu=4x\). For comparison, a structure at exactly the Kolmogorov scale has Reynolds number \(U_\eta\eta/\nu=1\), which \(Re_c=\beta^2\) reaches at \(\beta=1\).

Summary:

$$\gamma=\frac{4x\,\nu}{r_{\max}^2}=\frac{4x}{\beta^2}\,\gamma_\eta,\qquad \Gamma=\frac{2\pi\,r_{\max}U_{\max}}{1-e^{-x}}=8.78\,\beta^2\,\nu,\qquad R_\Gamma=\frac{\Gamma}{\nu}=8.78\,\beta^2 .$$

Step 5: strain share of the budget

Start from the background dissipation of section 5, \(\varepsilon_{\text{strain}}=3\nu\gamma^2\), and substitute \(\gamma\) from Step 2:

$$\varepsilon_{\text{strain}}=3\nu\left(\frac{4x}{\beta^2}\gamma_\eta\right)^2=\frac{48\,x^2}{\beta^4}\;\nu\gamma_\eta^2 .$$

Now \(\nu\gamma_\eta^2=\nu\cdot\varepsilon/\nu=\varepsilon\), so

$$\frac{\varepsilon_{\text{strain}}}{\varepsilon}=\frac{48\,x^2}{\beta^4}=\frac{75.8}{\beta^4}\qquad(48x^2=75.77).$$

Step 6: vortex share of the budget

Start from the vortex term of the section 6 budget, \(\varepsilon_{\text{vortex}}=0.977\,(L_eQ)\,U_{\max}^2\), where \(0.977=1/\left(2(1-e^{-x})^2\right)\) comes from section 4. Substitute in turn \(L_eQ=V_f\gamma\) (section 6), then \(\gamma=\frac{4x}{\beta^2}\gamma_\eta\) (Step 2) and \(U_{\max}^2=\beta^2U_\eta^2\):

$$\varepsilon_{\text{vortex}}=0.977\,V_f\,\gamma\,U_{\max}^2=0.977\,V_f\,\frac{4x}{\beta^2}\gamma_\eta\;\beta^2U_\eta^2=0.977\cdot4x\;V_f\;\gamma_\eta U_\eta^2 .$$

The factors \(\beta^2\) cancel, which is what the choice \(U_{\max}=\beta U_\eta\) buys. Next \(\gamma_\eta U_\eta^2=\sqrt{\varepsilon/\nu}\,\sqrt{\nu\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\), so

$$\frac{\varepsilon_{\text{vortex}}}{\varepsilon}=0.977\cdot4x\;V_f=4.91\,V_f .$$

Step 7: closing the budget and the volume fraction

The imposed dissipation is split between the background strain and the vortices, \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\text{strain}}+\varepsilon_{\text{vortex}}\). Dividing by \(\varepsilon\) and inserting Steps 5 and 6:

$$1=\frac{75.8}{\beta^4}+4.91\,V_f .$$

Solving for the volume fraction gives \(V_f\) as a function of the one dial \(\beta\):

$$\boxed{\;V_f=\frac{1-75.8/\beta^{4}}{4.91},\qquad r_{\max}=\beta\eta\;}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \beta=\left(\frac{75.8}{1-4.91\,V_f}\right)^{1/4}.$$

\(V_f\) must be positive, which needs \(\beta>75.8^{1/4}=2.95\), and cannot exceed \(1/4.91=20\%\) (the vortices would then carry all of \(\varepsilon\)).

Two more quantities complete the table. The inflow per metre of tube is the same for every \(\beta\):

$$Q=\pi\gamma r_{\max}^2=\pi\cdot4x\,\nu=15.8\,\nu ,$$

since \(\gamma r_{\max}^2=4x\nu\) (Step 1). The strain rate (small \(\gamma\)) and circulation (big \(\Gamma\)) follow from the summary of Step 4. Dimensional columns use the example \(\varepsilon=0.1\) W/kg and \(\nu=10^{-6}\) m²/s, for which \(\eta=56\ \mu\)m, \(U_\eta=17.8\) mm/s and \(\gamma_\eta=316\) s⁻¹.

Vortex length and spacing

The tube length per unit volume follows from \(L_e=V_f\gamma/Q\). At 1%: \(L_e=0.01\cdot178/1.58\times10^{-5}=1.1\times10^{5}\) m/m³, about 110 m of vortex per litre.

\(L_e\) has units m/m³ = 1/m², so each tube has on average \(1/L_e\) m² of cross-section to itself. For tubes roughly parallel and evenly spread, the mean spacing between axes is

$$d=\sqrt{\frac{V}{L}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_e}}\quad(L=L_eV\text{ metres of tube in a volume }V),$$

and with \(L_e=V_f/(\pi r_{\max}^2)\) from section 6:

$$d=r_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{V_f}}=\beta\,\eta\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{V_f}} .$$

So \(d/\eta\) depends on \(\beta\) and \(V_f\) only, not on \(\varepsilon\) or \(\nu\). For random orientation the spacing is of the same order; the exact factor depends on the orientation distribution.

Same example as above (\(\varepsilon=0.1\) W/kg, \(\nu=10^{-6}\) m²/s, \(\eta=56\ \mu\)m). The tubes are thin and well separated: even at 10% volume fraction the axes are about 20 Kolmogorov lengths apart, so a drop larger than about \(d\) intersects several tubes.

The strain term alone reaches 100% of \(\varepsilon\) at \(\beta=75.8^{1/4}=2.95\), so the tube radius is at least about \(3\eta\) and \(R_\Gamma\) is at least about 76. Any larger \(\beta\) hands the remainder to the vortex, and the volume fraction cannot exceed \(1/4.91=20\%\). A 20–25% vortex share needs \(V_f\approx5\%\), while the 1% quoted for worms gives about 5%.

8. A second closure: circulation set by the tube spacing

The budget leaves \(\beta\) free. A second relation comes from taking the circulation as the velocity difference across the mean spacing \(d\) (section 7) times that spacing, with the inertial-range velocity \(U(d)=(\varepsilon d)^{1/3}\):

$$\Gamma=c\,U(d)\,d=c\,\varepsilon^{1/3}d^{4/3}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\Gamma}{\nu}=c\left(\frac{d}{\eta}\right)^{4/3},$$

using \(\varepsilon^{1/3}\eta^{4/3}=\nu\). Insert \(\Gamma/\nu=8.78\,\beta^2\) (Step 4) and \(d/\eta=\beta\sqrt{\pi/V_f}\) (spacing section):

$$8.78\,\beta^2=c\,\beta^{4/3}\left(\frac{\pi}{V_f}\right)^{2/3}\;\Rightarrow\;\beta=\left(\frac{c}{8.78}\right)^{3/2}\frac{\pi}{V_f}.$$

Together with the budget \(1=75.8/\beta^4+4.91\,V_f\) this has one root \(V_f\) for each \(c\).

Letting \(c\) depend on \(\varepsilon\)

\(c\) is dimensionless, so it can depend on \(\varepsilon\) only through a Reynolds number; at fixed large scale \(L\) and \(\nu\) that number is \(\propto\varepsilon^{1/3}\). Try

$$c=c_0\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}\right)^{1/3},\qquad c_0=0.71\text{ at }\varepsilon_0=0.1\ \text{W/kg}.$$

The reference \(c_0=0.71\) is an assumed value, not fitted to data; it gives a vortex share of about 12% at 0.1 W/kg, in the range Moffatt quotes. Results for \(\nu=10^{-6}\) m²/s:

With \(c\propto\varepsilon^{1/3}\), \(V_f\) rises roughly as \(\varepsilon^{0.48}\) and the vortex share of the dissipation rises from about 4% to 34% over two decades of \(\varepsilon\). The tube radius stays near \(3\eta\) and \(R_\Gamma\) near 80–95, because the strain term pins \(\beta\) just above 2.95. Larger \(c_0\) pushes the share toward 100% and \(\beta\) away from 3 (for \(c_0=3\), 74% at 0.1 W/kg), so \(c_0\approx0.7\) is near the upper end that keeps the strain term dominant. The size of the \(\varepsilon\)-dependence is set entirely by the assumed exponent \(1/3\) and by \(c_0\). The inertial-range velocity is also questionable at \(d\approx20\)–\(47\eta\), inside the dissipation range of about \(60\eta\).

9. The data and their treatment

Sources

The radius and the swirl of vortex tubes were taken from 18 sources: simulations of forced isotropic turbulence (Jiménez et al. 1993; Kida et al. 2002; Pirozzoli 2009, 2012; Da Silva et al. 2011; Ishihara et al. 2011, 2013; Ghira et al. 2022, 2025), of mixing layers and channels (Tanahashi et al. 2001, 2004; Das et al. 2006; Wang et al. 2007), hot-wire and hot-film records (Belin et al. 1996; Mouri et al. 2003, 2004, 2007; Mouri and Hori 2009; Sassa and Makita 2005) and scanning PIV (Aligolzadeh et al. 2023). Each number was read from the rendered page of the paper and checked against the data file; the recording book shows the page, the number and the path to the value used. All values are expressed as the radius of maximum swirl of a Burgers vortex over \(\eta\) and the maximum swirl over \(U_\eta\) (the conversions are in the appendix, A0).

The sources select tubes in three ways, and this matters for what follows. Intense tubes are the connected regions of the 1% of the volume with the highest vorticity (Jiménez et al.; Da Silva et al.; Ghira et al.) or the events above a high threshold of a probe signal (the 0.1% and 1% averages of Mouri et al. 2004, 2007; Belin et al.). All tubes are found without a threshold, from the local flow pattern (Tanahashi et al.), the pressure (Kida et al.; Pirozzoli) or the average over all events of a probe record (Mouri and Hori).

Fig. 1. Radius and swirl of vortex tubes against \(Re_\lambda\), as used in the fits (open symbols: the value as calculated from the paper where a correction was applied; crosses: left out of the fits).

The data as read and as corrected by the models of the probes

Fig. 1b shows every row of the data against \(Re_\lambda\) on linear axes: above as read from the papers, below with the corrections that follow from the models: Ghira et al. (radius × 1.25, swirl × 0.67, section 9a) and the observed rows (Belin et al., Mouri et al. 2004, 2007, Mouri and Hori 2009, Sassa and Makita) with the multipliers of the wire-and-tube model and its one-dimensional extension (below; the multipliers are interpolated in \(\ln Re_\lambda\) from the table of each paper in the recording book), the other simulations as read. The all-tube average of Mouri and Hori does not state its amplitude threshold; its multiplier is that of the threshold \(k=0.33\) standard deviations of the increment, a choice inside the range 0.25 to 0.5 in which the model reproduces their values (over that range the swirl multiplier at \(Re_\lambda=2000\) changes by 28%). Rows with a range of \(Re_\lambda\) (the curves of Belin et al., the range of Mouri et al. 2003) are drawn as lines and are not used in the fits. Colour: blue for experiments, orange for simulations; each source has its own marker.

Fig. 1b. \(r_{\max}/\eta\), \(U_{\max}/U_\eta\) and \(G=\Gamma/\nu=8.784\,r_{\max}U_{\max}\) against \(Re_\lambda\), linear axes. Top: every row as read. Bottom: Ghira et al. and the observed rows corrected, the other simulations as read (open symbols: observed, no multiplier yet). Blue: experiments; orange: simulations. Dashed lines: the fits of this section, red without and grey with the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori (2009), whose dots are grey, as are the two rows of Sassa and Makita that no fit uses.

The radius and the swirl were fitted to the dots of the bottom row (50 points of 12 sources for the radius and 50 of 9 for the swirl; 61 and 61 with the rows of Mouri and Hori 2009), with the weighted sum of squares of the last appendix, in which every point has the same weight and the small and the large values are balanced; the standard error \(s\) of that appendix is quoted. Two kinds of dot are left out: the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori (2009) in the red fit, because it carries the largest multiplier and its threshold is not known (the grey fit includes it), and, in both fits, the two rows of Sassa and Makita at \(Re_\lambda=820\) (a shear flow) and 2391, grey in the figure. Radius: a straight line describes the radius better than a constant or a power law, \(r_{\max}/\eta=5.37-0.0004\,Re_\lambda\) without the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori (s = 0.117; a constant, 5.07, has s = 0.131) and \(5.33-0.0005\,Re_\lambda\) with it (s = 0.127); the line falls from 5.33 at \(Re_\lambda=100\) to 4.48 at 2000, a very small reduction over a wide range of Reynolds number, in simulations and experiments together. Swirl: \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=0.368\,Re_\lambda^{1/2}\) without and \(0.348\,Re_\lambda^{1/2}\) with the all-tube average (s = 0.134 and 0.167); the free exponent is 0.47 and 0.43 (s = 0.134 and 0.160), so 1/2 is as good as the free exponent. Because \(u'/U_\eta=Re_\lambda^{1/2}/15^{1/4}\), an exponent of 1/2 means that \(U_{\max}/u'=15^{1/4}\cdot0.368=0.72\) (0.68 with the all-tube average) does not depend on the Reynolds number: this is the scaling \(U_{\max}\propto u'\) that Mouri et al. (2007) found for the intense tubes of their experiments (reported by Mouri and Hori 2009, section 6), and Fig. 1b shows that it holds for simulations and experiments together over the range of the data. The circulation of the lines of the third panel is \(8.784\,r_{\max}U_{\max}\) of the two fits.

Corrections

Four corrections were adopted before the fits (the radius and the swirl of Mouri and Hori, the radius of Belin et al., the radius and the swirl of Ghira et al.); their rationale is given in full in the recording book (tab Corrections) and in appendix A0c.

The radius of the all-event hot-wire average (Mouri and Hori 2009), divided by 1.75. A probe crosses a tube along a chord at a random offset and tilt, so the mean profile of all events is wider than the tube; the authors say so and give no factor. A model of the crossing statistics (the chord model of appendix A0c, without the incidence angle; the wire-and-tube model below, applied to the method of Mouri and Hori with tubes of the DNS, gives a radius factor of 1.5–1.9 and a swirl factor of 2.4–3.8 at the thresholds that reproduce their averages, which supports the two factors) gives a ratio of 1.7 to 1.85. The corrected radii (4.7 to 5.3 \(\eta\)) agree with the simulations, and the fits are insensitive to the divisor between 1.6 and 1.9 (section 10).

The swirl of the same source, multiplied by 3, for the same reason: the chord model gives 2 to 3.5. The swirl of Ghira et al. (2022, 2025), multiplied by 0.67, to bring the swirl of the 1% most intense tubes to the whole population (section 9a; the factor 0.6 used before agrees with the level of the other sources at the same \(Re_\lambda\)). The threshold averages of Mouri et al. (2004, 2007) are left out, as tails of the distribution that the all-event average of Mouri and Hori contains whole.

The radius of Belin et al. (1996), divided by 1.15. The row is the median of their Fig. 5 (7.6 \(\eta\) as \(r_{\max}\)), not its peak, and the factor is the ratio of the radius read to the true radius of the intense tubes in the wire-and-tube model below (1.06 at \(Re_\lambda=151\) to 1.18 at 718); the corrected radius is 6.6 \(\eta\) (provisional: it rests on the tubes found from their own records, which the one-dimensional methods of Mouri et al. and of Sassa and Makita do not support, section 9). Their swirl, \(\Delta S/(2\sin\alpha)\) with \(\sin\alpha=0.14\), is too high by a factor of about 2.6 in the model, and the model value is itself about three times the DNS law; it is not a row of the table.

The radius of Ghira et al. (2022, 2025), multiplied by 1.25. The strongest 1% of the volume by vorticity is a subset of the tubes, smaller and faster than the whole population. The factors are worked out in section 9a, in steps, from the all-tube population of Pirozzoli (2012), chosen as the reference because it has no lower threshold on the vorticity: his pdfs of the radius and of the maximum velocity are linked by his most frequent circulation (\(\Gamma/\nu=80\)), the cut of Ghira et al. is applied with the tubes filling 35% of the flow, and the multipliers are the value of the reference (the narrow family of the radius pdf, all tubes for the swirl) over that of the kept tubes: 1.22 to 1.28 for the radius and 0.66 to 0.68 for the swirl. The corrected radius is 5.6 to 6.2 \(\eta\) and the swirl is multiplied by 0.67 in place of 0.6.

Review of the corrections. The two swirl factors are the weakest numbers of the data set, for three reasons found in the review. First, Da Silva et al. (2011), whose swirl (3.7 and 4.3 \(U_\eta\), from their \(u_0/u'\)) was a support of the factor 0.6 of the swirl of Ghira et al. (now 0.67, section 9a), print \(\langle u_0\rangle/u_\eta=9.0\) and 7.15 in the same table, and their circulation implies 10.5; the paper does not resolve the factor 2.5, and its swirl is therefore not fitted. Secondly, without any factor the intense-tube sources agree with each other: Ghira et al. (simulation) and the 0.1% averages of Mouri et al. (2007, hot wire) lie on one line. Thirdly, the all-tube sources alone (Kida et al. and Mouri and Hori) are best joined with a swirl factor of 1.84, not 3. These points do not affect the radius. They are taken up in section 12.

The review also moved Tanahashi et al. (2001) from an assumed \(Re_\lambda=200\) to 80 (their Fig. 1b), and added the swirl of the \(Re_\lambda=54\) runs of Ghira et al. (2025) and the circulation of Jiménez et al. (1993).

The width of the distributions

The values above are means or peaks of distributions. The probability densities of the diameter and the swirl of all tubes were digitised from Tanahashi et al. (2001, 2004), Das et al. (2006) and Pirozzoli (2012) (recording book). Each radius distribution is the sum of two lognormal functions. The first is narrow (width 0.29 to 0.35) and holds 53 to 71% of the tubes; its median is 5.2, 4.9 and 4.3 \(\eta\) and its mean 5.5, 5.3 and 4.6 \(\eta\) in Tanahashi et al. (2001), Tanahashi et al. (2004) and Pirozzoli (2012). This first lognormal is the tube of the model: \(r_{\max}/\eta\approx5\), the value found for the intense tubes and for the corrected probe data. The second lognormal is broad (width 0.6 to 0.7), with a median of 8.5 to 16.8 \(\eta\), two to three times the first; it raises the mean of the whole distribution to 7.2 to 8.2 \(\eta\) although the peak stays at 4.2 to 4.8. The open-symbol data of Das et al. (2006), from the centre of a channel at \(Re_\tau=180\), show almost only the broad function. What the second family is (larger tubes, or sheets and tubes in formation that the eduction also counts) is not settled; section 14 returns to it.

The wire-and-tube model of a hot-wire crossing

The experimental rows of the table (Belin et al., Mouri et al., Sassa and Makita) are not measurements of tubes: they are what a wire reads as tubes are carried past it, converted back to a tube by a rule. The earlier version of this correction (appendix A0c, the chord model) took a tube, a straight path through it at a random offset and tilt, and a sensed component, and reproduced the size distribution of Belin et al. only with a swirl at or above the speed of the disks. The cause was found in the paper of Belin et al. itself (their Fig. 3 and eqs. 2–8): the wire is cooled by the velocity normal to it, and the tube crosses the wire at a small angle \(\alpha\) to that direction. The model that follows adds that angle and the cooling law, and replaces the weights of the old model by the geometry of a volume of tubes.

Tube. A straight Burgers vortex, \(v_\theta(\rho)=\omega_0R^2\,(1-e^{-\rho^2/2R^2})/\rho\), \(r_{\max}=1.585R\), \(U_{\max}=0.4512\,\omega_0R\), circulation \(\Gamma=8.784\,r_{\max}U_{\max}\), with an isotropic axis. Wire. A fixed wire along \(y\); the mean flow \(U=0.588\,\Omega R\) of the table (recording book, tab Belin) is along \(x\), normal to the wire. A tube is carried with the velocity \(\mathbf W=\mathbf U+\mathbf w\), where \(\mathbf w\) is the large-scale fluctuation along the wire (rms \(u'\)); the incidence angle \(\alpha\) is the angle between \(\mathbf W\) and \(x\), \(\tan\alpha=w/U\), so \(\sin\alpha\) is random with a standard deviation \(u'/U=0.29\), the same at every \(Re_\lambda\) in the table. By Taylor's hypothesis the time is a distance, \(s=|\mathbf W|\,t\). The wire cools with the speed

$$U_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sqrt{|\mathbf u|^2-(1-k^2)\,(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf e_w)^2},\qquad \mathbf u=\mathbf U+\mathbf v,$$

with the yaw coefficient \(k=0.2\) (the velocity along the wire cools it only a little), and the signal is \(S=U_{\mathrm{eff}}-U_{\mathrm{eff}}(\text{no tube})\). To first order the wire reads the component of the swirl along its normal direction, and for a tube whose axis is normal to \(\mathbf W\) and to the wire, crossed through its axis,

$$S(s)=\sin\alpha\;\mathrm{sgn}(s)\,v_\theta(|s|),\qquad \Delta S=2\sin\alpha\,U_{\max},$$

two extrema \(3.17R\) apart (Belin et al., eq. 7). Without the angle there is almost no S-shape: for such a tube the swirl at the wire is perpendicular to the path. Reading. Belin et al. read \(r_{\max}=\tfrac12\Delta s\) from the spacing of the extrema and \(U_{\max}=\Delta S/(2\sin\alpha)\) with the constant \(\sin\alpha=0.14\) (8°, estimated from the signal); the model applies the same rules to its own signals.

Which tubes the wire meets. Tubes of length \(L\gg R\) fill a volume. A tube whose closest approach to the wire is closer than the largest distance at which it can still pass the detection threshold, \(b_{\max}=\sqrt{\Gamma/(2\pi G_c)}\), can be detected (the velocity gradient of a line vortex is at most \(\Gamma/2\pi b^2\) outside the core); the number of tubes of a class met per unit time is the flow past the wire times the number of tubes per volume times their footprint in the plane normal to the flow, \(2b_{\max}L\cos(\text{tilt})\). The length \(L\) cancels in the distribution. A tube is therefore met in proportion to its detection range, not to its radius, and no tube that can be selected is dropped. Selection. Belin et al. keep the events at the far tails of the velocity derivative (area \(2.6\times10^{-3}\)), a velocity gradient above five standard deviations, \(|dS/ds|\ge5\,U_\eta/(\sqrt{15}\,\eta)\); an event is read when its signal has a maximum and a minimum within \(\pm2r_{\max}\) of the steepest point.

Inputs and fit. The radius \(r_{\max}/\eta\) is lognormal, and the swirl is a scale \(S\) times the DNS value \(0.769\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}U_\eta\) with a lognormal spread; the two are independent. Fitting the size pdf (Fig. 5 of Belin et al.) and the pdf of the product \(Re_f/Re_\lambda^{1/2}\) (Fig. 6) at \(Re_\lambda=255\) and 659, in three phases (the radius alone, the swirl alone, all four), gives a radius median of 7.29 \(\eta\) (ln-width 0.58) and a swirl 2.58 times the DNS value (ln-width 0.38). The flow quantities (\(\nu\), \(\varepsilon\), \(U_\eta\), \(U\), \(u'\)) come from the correlations of Table I of Belin et al. (recording book, tab Belin).

Fig. W1. The model fitted to Belin et al. (1996) at \(Re_\lambda=659\) (the same fit at 255 is in the recording book). Top left: the radius, the tubes as generated (grey), the tubes that hit the wire (blue), the intense tubes (dashed) and the radius as read (red) against Fig. 5; top right: the product \(r_{\max}U_{\max}\) as \(x=Re_f/Re_\lambda^{1/2}\) against Fig. 6; bottom: \(U_{\max}\) in cm/s and in \(U_\eta\): (i) generated, (ii) hit the wire, (ii') hit, selected and read, (iii) observed by the wire (\(\Delta S/2\)), (iv) with Belin's \(\sin\alpha=0.14\), (v) with the actual \(\alpha\) of each event.

What the model says about the experiment. (1) The incidence angle makes the signal: the wire observes only \(\sin\alpha\,U_{\max}\), a median of 8.1 \(U_\eta\) against the true median of 22.9 \(U_\eta\) of the events that are read; with \(\alpha=0\) only 1% of the selected events could be read. (2) The events that are read and selected have large angles (median \(|\sin\alpha|=0.39\), against 0.19 over all crossings), so Belin's constant 0.14 overstates their swirl by a factor of 2.5; with the actual angle the median is 21.7 \(U_\eta\), on the true value. (3) The cut favours strong tubes: the swirl of the tubes that are read is 1.3 times that of all tubes. (4) The radius that Belin reads is a little too large: the ratio of the radius read to the true radius of the same events is 1.06 at \(Re_\lambda=151\) and 1.18 at 718. (5) The fit needs a swirl 2.6 times the DNS value (34 cm/s at \(Re_\lambda=659\); the speed of the disks is 154 cm/s), and the radius pdf is narrower at the peak than Fig. 5; both are open (below).

Fig. W2. The tubes behind the records of Belin et al. (the model of Fig. W1 at \(Re_\lambda=659\): all tubes, grey, and the intense tubes that are selected and read, dashed) against the pdfs of Tanahashi et al. (2001) (orange, two lognormals fitted to their digitised pdfs, \(Re_\lambda\approx80\)). (a) \(r_{\max}/\eta\); (b) \(U_{\max}/u'\).

Comparison with the DNS. The radius of the tubes found from the hot-wire pdfs is that of the DNS: median 7.3 and mean 8.6 \(\eta\) for all tubes (Tanahashi et al.: 5.8 and 7.8), and 6.3 and 6.9 for the intense tubes, close to the narrow lognormal of the DNS at about 5 \(\eta\) that the closure uses. The swirl is not: the median \(U_{\max}/u'\) of all tubes is 1.32 and of the intense tubes 1.76, against 0.75 of Tanahashi et al. (a factor 1.8 and 2.3); in units of \(U_\eta\) the intense tubes have 23 at \(Re_\lambda=659\), about three times the law \(0.77\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}\). Three assumptions bear on this and are not tested by the pdfs of Belin et al.: the Gaussian spread of \(\sin\alpha\) with \(u'/U\), the independence of radius and swirl, and the use of one pdf (Fig. 6) pooled over \(Re_\lambda=151\)–718 for two Reynolds numbers.

The DNS law of this section, \(U_{\max}=0.769\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}U_\eta\), is the coefficient of the selected law at the time the model was fitted; the selection of section 10 now gives 0.834 (after the swirl rows of Jiménez et al., the factors of Ghira et al. of section 9a and the other changes of the data). The multipliers of this section and of the recording book were computed with 0.769 and were not recomputed; the effect of the difference on them was not tested.

The one-dimensional methods of Mouri et al. and Sassa and Makita on the model tubes

The hot-wire rows of the table come from three methods that average the signals of the events found by a threshold. All three use a crossed wire and the transverse velocity (the spanwise \(v\) of Mouri et al., the vertical \(w\) of Sassa and Makita), which is linear in the swirl and needs no incidence angle. Mouri et al. (2007) take the increment \(v(x+\delta x_s/2)-v(x-\delta x_s/2)\) over the sampling interval, keep the events above the threshold that holds 0.1% or 1% of all increments (6.0–6.7 and 3.5–3.7 standard deviations, their Table II), align and average the signals and fit the mean profile with the Burgers vortex around its peaks (\(R_0\), \(V_0\)). Mouri and Hori (2009) take all local extrema of the Gaussian-smoothed increment over \(6\eta\), above the background, and do the same. Sassa and Makita (2005) keep the events with \(dw/dt\ge C\,\mathrm{rms}(dw/dt)\), \(C=2.5\), and read the diameter and the maximum velocity from the two peaks of the mean trace. The wire-and-tube model above gives these methods a population to act on: the transverse component of the swirl along the path of the mean flow, smoothed by the probe (1 mm for Mouri et al., about \(\eta\) for Sassa and Makita), the thresholds in units of the rms increment \(\sqrt{2/15}\,(U_\eta/\eta)\,\delta x\) of the dissipative range, and the same weights, so the three methods are applied to the same model as the wire of Belin et al. There is no background turbulence in the model.

The result. Tubes of the DNS (\(r_{\max}\approx5.2\,\eta\) with a narrow lognormal width of 0.3, and \(U_{\max}=0.769\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}U_\eta\) times a lognormal of width 0.4, no scale factor) reproduce the three methods. (1) Mouri et al. (2007), 0.1%: \(V_0/u_K\) at \(Re_\lambda=332, 719, 1098, 1934\) is 8.0, 9.5, 10.7, 13.5 in the model against 7.6, 8.7, 10.0, 14.0 in the paper, and \(R_0/\eta\) is 5.1, 5.6, 6.3, 8.3 against 5.2, 5.2, 5.6, 6.2. 1%: \(V_0/u_K\) is 5.7, 6.8, 7.5, 9.1 against 5.6, 6.1, 6.8, 9.2, and \(R_0/\eta\) 5.8, 6.2, 6.8, 8.5 against 6.5, 6.5, 6.6, 7.0. (2) Sassa and Makita (2005): the maximum velocity of the mean trace is 2.8 \(u_K\) at \(Re_\lambda=19\), 4.6 at 300 and 7.0 at 2391, against 2.8, 4.2 and 6.5 in the paper (the shear flow at 820 is lower in the paper, 2.1, than the model, 5.6), and the diameter is 10, 12, 14 \(\eta\) against their value of about 10 \(\eta\). (3) Mouri and Hori (2009), all tubes: the all-tube average is reproduced when the threshold is very low, 0.25–0.5 standard deviations of the increment over \(6\eta\): \(R_0/\eta=8.1, 8.5, 9.0, 10.5\) and \(V_0/u_K=2.7, 3.1, 3.4, 3.8\) for the threshold 0.5 at \(Re_\lambda=332, 719, 1098, 1934\), against 8.4, 8.6, 8.9, 8.8 and 2.4, 2.4, 2.6, 3.2 in the paper (the threshold 0.25 gives 8.9, 9.4, 9.9, 11.5 and 2.1, 2.5, 2.7, 2.9). The true radius of the same events is 5.4 \(\eta\) and the true swirl 6.4–11.4 \(U_\eta\) (\(Re_\lambda=332\)–1934). The ratios of the model are, for the thresholds 0.5 and 0.25, a radius factor of 1.49–1.92 and 1.62–2.10 and a swirl factor of 2.4–3.0 and 3.0–3.8; the corrections adopted in this paper for Mouri and Hori, 1.75 and 3, lie inside these ranges.

Fig. W3. The three one-dimensional methods applied to model tubes. Blue: tubes of the DNS (\(r_{\max}\approx5\,\eta\), \(U_{\max}\) of the DNS); red dashed: the tubes found from Belin et al. (median \(r_{\max}\) 7.3 \(\eta\), \(U_{\max}\) 2.6 times the DNS); open black symbols: the papers. Circles: the 0.1% class (Mouri et al. 2007), squares: 1%, triangles: all tubes at the threshold of 2 standard deviations (the paper's all-tube average needs 0.25–0.5, see the text). Right: the diameter of the mean trace of Sassa and Makita (2005).

What this says. (1) The three one-dimensional methods and the DNS tubes agree: a radius of about \(5\,\eta\) and a swirl of the DNS law, \(0.77\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}U_\eta\), explain the 0.1% and 1% classes of Mouri et al., the mean trace of Sassa and Makita and, with a threshold at the level of the background, the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori. The tubes found from the records of Belin et al. do not: with the same methods they read radii and velocities 1.5 to 5 times too high (Fig. W3). The record of Belin et al. is the outlier of the data, and its amplitude needs tubes 2.6 times stronger than the DNS with the wire model above, also with a wider spread of the incidence angle (\(\sin\alpha\) of width 0.6: 2.4 times). (2) The relation between the classes, at \(Re_\lambda=719\): the radius read is 1.21 (0.1%), 1.26 (1%) and 1.55 (all tubes, threshold 0.5) times the true radius of the events, and the swirl read is 0.77, 0.68 and 0.38 times the true swirl, so that a high threshold reads near-axis crossings (and smaller, stronger tubes: the true radius of the events falls and the true swirl rises with the threshold). (3) The two chord factors of this paper, radius divided by 1.75 and swirl multiplied by 3 for the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori, are supported by a model with one-dimensional geometry only; the threshold of the all-tube average is not given in the paper and is the one free quantity (0.25–0.5 standard deviations). Limits: no background turbulence in the model (the lowest thresholds are where it matters most), radius and swirl independent, and one smoothing length for the probe.

9a. DNS PDF

The probability densities of the radius and of the swirl of the tubes were digitised from every DNS and scanning-PIV paper that prints them (Tanahashi et al. 2001, 2004; Das et al. 2006; Pirozzoli 2012; Wang et al. 2007; Ghira et al. 2022; Jiménez and Wray 1998; Aligolzadeh et al. 2023), each from the figure of the paper (recording book, with the digitised curve drawn over the figure). The radius is that of each paper: \(D/2\) of the coherent eddy (Tanahashi, Das, Wang), \(r_0\) of the core (Pirozzoli), the \(1/e\) radius \(R_{ivs}\) or \(R\) of the vorticity of the intense structures (Ghira, Jiménez) and the radius \(R/\eta\) of the structure boundary (Aligolzadeh). Every curve was scaled to unit area; the area of the curve as digitised, 0.94 to 1.06, checks the axes. Ghira et al. (2022) are read from the vector paths of the pdf, so for them the check is exact.

Each curve was fitted with one lognormal function, \(p(x)=\exp[-(\ln x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2]/(x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\), median \(m=e^{\mu}\), and with a sum of two, \(a_1p_1+(1-a_1)p_2\) (the function of the page, the first the narrow one, widths at most 0.7 for the radius). The sum of two is kept only where its rms misfit (divided by the peak) is below 0.7 times that of the single one; this threshold is our choice, and the entries with a ratio between 0.65 and 0.8 (the swirl of Tanahashi et al. 2004, 0.69, of Wang et al., 0.66, and of Pirozzoli, 0.75, and the two histograms of Aligolzadeh et al., 0.80 and 0.75) would change with it. Where \(n=1\), \(a_1=1\) and there is no second lognormal. \(m\) is in \(\eta\) for the radius and in \(u_K\) or \(u'\) for the swirl.

The pdfs without a volume threshold (Tanahashi, Das, Pirozzoli, Wang) are sums of two lognormals: a narrow family of median 4.3 to 6.2 \(\eta\) and width 0.23 to 0.35, and a broad one of median 8.5 to 17 \(\eta\) and width 0.6 to 0.7, which is the long tail of Fig. D1 and carries the mean to 7.2 to 10.2 \(\eta\). The sets that select the intense tubes by a threshold on the volume (Ghira et al., 1%; Jiménez and Wray) and the PIV histograms of Aligolzadeh et al. have no such tail: the seven runs of Ghira et al. are one lognormal each, of median 4.14 (\(Re_\lambda=90\)) falling to 3.73 \(\eta\) (399) and width 0.26 to 0.28. In Fig. D3 (one point per pdf, always its first lognormal, so that the same family is compared across the sets) the radius points have \(\mu=1.04\) to 1.82 (median 2.8 to 6.2 \(\eta\)) and \(\sigma=0.13\) to 0.50. There is no one relation between \(\sigma\) and \(\mu\): over the 15 points the correlation is only 0.45 (0.41 over the 9 sources, the seven runs of Ghira et al. counted as one); within the thresholded sets it is +0.85 (\(\sigma\approx-0.49+0.57\mu\), 10 points) and within the unthresholded sets \(-0.85\) (5 points), whose narrow lognormals cluster at \(\mu=1.46\) to 1.82 and \(\sigma=0.23\) to 0.35 (median 4.3 to 6.2 \(\eta\)). The swirl pdfs are too few to give a trend: the first lognormals of the four pdfs in \(u_K\) are alike (median 1.9 to 2.3 \(u_K\), \(\sigma=0.62\) to 0.77) and those of the three in \(u'\) have \(\sigma=0.54\) to 0.86 (median 0.29 to 0.64 \(u'\)), the curve of Tanahashi et al. (2001) being in both units.

The correction of the 1%-volume DNS (Ghira et al.), in steps

The DNS of Ghira et al. (2022, 2025) keep the strongest 1% of the volume by vorticity: a subset of the tubes, smaller and faster than the whole population. To bring it to the whole population we chose Pirozzoli (2012) as the reference, because his pdfs of the core radius and of the maximum velocity are of all the vortex cores found, with no lower threshold on the vorticity (his only selections are an angle of at most 20° between the vorticity and the plane normal and a clear swirling pattern), and worked out the scaling factors from it, in the steps below, with the tubes filling 35% of the flow.

  1. The row to correct. The row of Ghira et al. is the mean \(r_{\max}\) and \(U_{\max}\) of the structures above the vorticity \(\omega_c\) that holds the strongest 1% of the volume: \(r_{\max}=4.5\) to 5.0 \(\eta\) (\(1.12\,R_{ivs}/(R_{ivs}/R_B)\)), the swirl converted to the Burgers peak.
  2. The reference. Pirozzoli (2012), Fig. 2: the pdf of the radius \(r_0\) (mean 7.2 \(\eta\) over the range digitised, median 5.3, most frequent 4.2; the text says 'expected value about 6'; a narrow family of 53% of the tubes with mean 4.55 \(\eta\) and a broad family with median 8.5 \(\eta\) whose far tail sets the mean) and of the maximum velocity \(v_0\) (mean 2.5 \(u_K\); the text says about 2).
  3. The vorticity of a tube. A Burgers vortex has \(\omega(\rho)=\omega_0\,e^{-\rho^2/2R^2}\), \(R=r_{\max}/1.585\) and \(\omega_0=3.512\,U_{\max}/r_{\max}\) in units of \(1/\tau_\eta\), which is the rms vorticity of homogeneous isotropic turbulence (\(\varepsilon=\nu\langle\omega^2\rangle\)).
  4. Pairing the radius with the swirl. His pdfs are separate, but his text gives the most frequent circulation, \(\Gamma_\infty/\nu=80\), with \(\Gamma_0=2\pi r_0v_0=0.715\,\Gamma_\infty\), so \(G=\Gamma_\infty/\nu=8.784\,r\,U\) and \(U=G/(8.784\,r)\): a small tube is fast, \(\omega_0\) falls roughly as \(1/r^2\). Two versions bracket the spread of \(G\): (a) \(G\) constant, 80 or 94; (b) \(r\) and \(G\) independent, with \(\mathrm{var}\ln G=\mathrm{var}\ln U-\mathrm{var}\ln r=0.49-0.40=0.09\) (the swirl pdf as the lognormal of median 2.0 and ln-width 0.70, the radius pdf as its two lognormals), which gives \(\ln r\) and \(\ln U\) a correlation of \(-0.9\).
  5. The 1% of the volume. A tube of length \(L\) has the volume \(\pi\rho_c^2L=2\pi R^2L\ln(\omega_0/\omega_c)\) inside the surface where its vorticity falls to \(\omega_c\) (\(\rho_c=R\sqrt{2\ln(\omega_0/\omega_c)}\)), and the volume \(\pi r_{\max}^2L\) out to \(r_{\max}\). The cut \(\omega_c\) is fixed so that the volume above it is 1% of the flow when all the tubes fill 35% of it (Kida et al.: 0.31 to 0.35): the sum of the first volumes over the sum of the second is 0.01/0.35.
  6. The tubes that are kept. At 35% about 45% of the tubes are kept, those of small radius (version a: \(r<4.9\,\eta\)), of mean radius 3.6 to 3.7 \(\eta\) and mean swirl 2.7 to 3.8 \(u_K\) (Table D3), with a mean axis vorticity of 3.2 to 4.3 against the 3.9 to 4.8 of Ghira et al. (Table III). 71% to 77% of them belong to the narrow family of the radius pdf, which they represent (23% to 43% of the broad family is kept as well).
  7. The multipliers are the value of the reference over the value of the kept tubes. Radius: the mean of the narrow family, 4.55 \(\eta\), over the mean radius of the kept tubes, \(f_R=4.55/3.56=1.28\) (a) and \(4.55/3.72=1.22\) (b). Swirl: the mean of all the tubes over that of the kept tubes, \(f_U=0.68\) (a) and 0.66 (b).
  8. Used: radius multiplied by 1.25 and swirl by 0.67, for Ghira et al. (2022, 2025). At other fillings the factors are 1.12 to 1.16 and 0.71 to 0.73 (20%) and 1.0 and 0.8 (10%).

What fixes the result. (1) The radius target. The vorticity cut cannot see the large tubes of the broad family, and the narrow family is the tube of the model, so the radius is brought to the narrow family; brought to the mean of all the tubes (7.2 \(\eta\), and 6 in his text) the factor would be 1.7 to 2.0, and the fits are then much worse (below). (2) The filling \(\varphi\). It is an input; its range in the literature is the one quoted. (3) The pairing. Independent \(r\) and \(U\) would give a most frequent \(G\) of 44, not his 80, so a negative correlation of \(\ln r\) and \(\ln U\) (\(-0.9\) in version b) is needed.

Limits. The pdfs are those of one population at one \(Re_\lambda\) (251, the open circles of his Fig. 2; the caption says case D, 98.6), the runs of Ghira et al. cover 90 to 399, and their structures are larger than the kept tubes of the model (\(r_{\max}\) of 4.5 to 5.0 \(\eta\) against 3.6 to 3.7), so the corrected radius, 5.6 to 6.2 \(\eta\), lies above the narrow family. The consequence in the fits (section 10): with the radius of Ghira et al. multiplied by 1.25 and the swirl by 0.67 the rms misfit of the best models is 11% and the leave-one-source-out error 12% to 14%; with the radius as listed they are 10% and 11% to 13%, and with the radius multiplied by 1.85 (the mean of all the tubes as the target) 19% to 22% and 22% to 24%.

10. Selection of the model

Candidate models express \(r_{\max}/\eta\) and \(U_{\max}/U_\eta\) as functions of \(Re_\lambda\) with one to four parameters: a constant radius or one that varies as a power or a logarithm of \(Re_\lambda\), and a swirl that is a power law, a power law with a fixed exponent (1/2: proportional to the r.m.s. velocity; 1/3), a logarithmic law, or that follows from a law for the circulation. Each is fitted by least squares of the logarithmic residuals of the radius (32 points) and the swirl (26 points), every source having the same weight in each quantity (15 source-quantity groups).

An earlier version chose the model with the fewest parameters within 25% of the best root-mean-square (rms) residual; the width of that band has no basis. Here the choice is made by cross-validation: each source in turn is left out, the model is fitted to the others and predicts the one left out, and the rms of those prediction errors (LOSO, in per cent) is the score. A parameter that follows the noise of one source worsens the score, so complexity is penalised by the data. The Akaike criterion with small-sample correction (AICc) and the Bayesian criterion (BIC), with a source-quantity group as the unit of data, are given for comparison; differences below 2 carry no evidence (Burnham and Anderson 2002).

The model D6 (radius 5, swirl c Re^(1/3) (exponent fixed); 1 parameter) predicts left-out sources best, 12.3%; L2 (2 parameters) follows at 12.7%, D8 (3 parameters) follows at 12.7%, L1 (2 parameters) follows at 13.5%, L3 (3 parameters) follows at 13.5%. No model with three or four parameters predicts better than D6: the best of them, D8, scores 12.7%, so a fitted radius, a radius that varies with \(Re_\lambda\) or a free exponent add nothing that survives leaving a source out. With complexity penalised, the model with the fewest parameters among the best is selected. The logarithmic law, \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=-3.45+1.63\ln Re_\lambda\), is equivalent within the range of the data (L1, 13.5%) but turns negative below \(Re_\lambda\approx8\).

The selection is robust to the radius divisor of Mouri and Hori (the score of D6 is 12.4% to 12.5% for 1.6 to 1.9) and fragile to the factors of Ghira et al. (Table 2). With their swirl as listed no single law predicts left-out sources better than 20%, whatever its number of parameters: the single law exists only with both swirl factors. The radius of Ghira et al. matters as well: multiplied by 1.85 (the mean of all tubes as the target) the best score is 22.3%, with the adopted 1.25 12.3%, as listed 10.8%.

11. The selected single-population model (model I)

$$r_{\max}=5\,\eta,\qquad \frac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=0.834\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}$$

and, from sections 3 to 7 with \(\beta=5\),

$$\frac{\gamma}{\gamma_\eta}=\frac{4x}{\beta^2}=0.201,\qquad \frac{\Gamma}{\nu}=8.78\,\beta\,\frac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta},\qquad V_f=\left(1-\frac{75.8}{\beta^4}\right)\frac{\beta^2}{4.91\,(U_{\max}/U_\eta)^2},\qquad \frac{d}{\eta}=\beta\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{V_f}} .$$

The rms residual is 11.4% for the radius and 11.4% for radius and swirl together. The swirl dissipation of the tubes is 0.88 of the total at \(\beta=5\), the remainder being the dissipation of the background strain; the volume fraction \(V_f\) follows from this balance and is a prediction, not a fit.

Fig. 2. Model I with the data (corrected as in section 9).

12. A two-population reading (model II)

Plotted as calculated from the papers, without any swirl correction, the data form two families (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3. The swirl as calculated from the papers. Red: the most intense tubes. Blue: all tubes; the open diamonds are Mouri and Hori (2009) as printed, the filled diamonds the same times the fitted chord factor.

Intense tubes. The 1% most intense tubes of simulations (Ghira et al. 2022, 2025; \(Re_\lambda\) 54 to 399) and the 0.1% threshold averages of hot-wire records (Mouri et al. 2007; 332 to 1934) follow one law over 20 points without correction,

$$\frac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}\bigg|_{\text{intense}}=1.29\,Re_\lambda^{0.32}\qquad(\text{rms }12\%),$$

close to a constant fraction of the r.m.s. velocity at the Reynolds numbers of the simulations, as their authors report. The values printed by Da Silva et al. (9.0 and 7.15) lie on this family.

All tubes. The low-pressure vortices of Kida et al. (2002) and the all-event averages of Mouri and Hori (2009), with one fitted factor for the chord effect on the swirl, give

$$\frac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}\bigg|_{\text{all}}=2.00\,Re_\lambda^{0.13},\qquad\text{chord factor }1.84\qquad(\text{rms }1.3\%).$$

The exponent within Mouri and Hori alone is 0.15 and within Kida et al. alone 0.09; a chord factor of 3 forces an exponent of 0.33 that neither source shows (rms 3.9%). The fitted factor 1.84 lies at the low end of the chord model (2 to 3.5). This is what Mouri and Hori state: the swirl of all tubes scales with the Kolmogorov velocity, that of intense tubes with the r.m.s. velocity.

Checks with data not used in a fit. Kida et al. measured the volume fraction of their vortex cores: 0.35 at \(Re_\lambda=83\) and 0.31 at 170. The budget of section 7 gives 0.35 and 0.29 with the all-tube swirl of model II, and 0.34 and 0.21 with model I. Sassa and Makita (2005), who sample events at a moderate threshold between \(Re_\lambda=19\) and 2391, report an exponent 0.28 for the swirl, between the two families. The mean swirl of all tubes in the mixing layer of Tanahashi et al. (2001; \(Re_\lambda\approx80\)) is 3.7 \(U_\eta\) (model II: 3.6); that of Pirozzoli (2012; \(Re_\lambda\approx99\), the test case D named in the caption of his Fig. 2) is 2.5 (model II: 3.7); the plotted symbols are those of his case E (\(Re_\lambda=251\); model II: 4.1), so the disagreement remains whichever case it is.

Which model. Model I is the simplest description of the corrected data and is retained as the reference. Model II rests on fewer adjustments (one fitted factor against two), agrees with what the authors of the hot-wire papers conclude, and reproduces the measured volume fraction at both Reynolds numbers; its weakness is that the all-tube law rests on two sources. The two differ little near \(Re_\lambda\approx100\), where most simulations are, and by a factor 1.68 in the swirl at \(Re_\lambda=1000\) (Table 3). For a closure of micromixing, which depends on all tubes weighted by their volume, we recommend model II and regard the difference between the two as the uncertainty of the swirl at high Reynolds number. The intense tubes, if they keep 1% of the volume, carry 6% of the dissipation at \(Re_\lambda=100\) and a growing share above (Table 3, last column).

13. Use as a closure in CFD, and the delay of the cascade

The closure

A Reynolds-averaged or large-eddy solver provides the turbulent kinetic energy \(k\) and the dissipation rate \(\varepsilon\) in each cell (in a large-eddy simulation, the subgrid values). With \(u'^2=2k/3\) and isotropic small scales,

$$Re_\lambda=\sqrt{\frac{20}{3}}\,\frac{k}{\sqrt{\nu\varepsilon}},\qquad \eta=\left(\frac{\nu^3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/4},\qquad \tau_\eta=\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\varepsilon}} .$$

The tubes in the cell then have the radius \(r_{\max}=5\eta\), the stretching rate \(\gamma=0.201/\tau_\eta\), the swirl of model I or II, and the circulation, volume fraction and spacing of section 11. These are the quantities a micromixing model needs: \(\gamma\) is the rate at which a fluid element in a tube is thinned, \(d\) the distance over which fresh fluid must be brought to a tube, \(\Gamma/\nu\) the Reynolds number of the engulfing motion. The engulfment rate of Bałdyga and Bourne, \(E=0.058\,(\varepsilon/\nu)^{1/2}\), is \(0.29\,\gamma\), and the vortex size they assumed, \(12\,\eta\), is the tube diameter \(2r_{\max}=10\,\eta\): the closure gives their model a measured basis and adds the dependence on \(Re_\lambda\) through the swirl and the volume fraction.

The closure applies where the small scales are in local equilibrium with \(\varepsilon\) and \(Re_\lambda\) is within the data (35 to about 2000). Stirred tanks and jets at process scale are within this range; near walls and at interfaces the tubes are aligned and somewhat wider (Tanahashi et al. 2004), which the closure does not represent.

The delay between energy input and dissipation

The closure is local in time: it takes the tubes to follow \(\varepsilon\) at once. They cannot. Energy put into the large scales reaches the dissipative scales only after it has passed down the cascade, and the dissipation in the tubes lags the input. In forced turbulence the dissipation follows the energy input with a delay of the order of a large-eddy turnover time (Pearson et al. 2004); in decaying turbulence the transit takes about half an initial turnover time (Yoffe and McComb 2018); and where the large scales change faster than this, the dissipation departs from its equilibrium scaling altogether (Vassilicos 2015; Goto and Vassilicos 2016). In a stirred tank a fluid element passes the impeller stream in a time comparable with the turnover time of the eddies made there, so the tubes that perform the micromixing downstream were fed by the energy input upstream.

The transit time follows from the cascade itself. An eddy of size \(\ell\) hands its energy on in its turnover time \(\ell^{2/3}\varepsilon^{-1/3}\). Integrating \(d\ell/dt=-a\,\ell^{1/3}\varepsilon^{1/3}\) from the energy-containing scale \(L=u'^3/\varepsilon\) to the tube radius \(\beta\eta\) gives

$$T_c=\frac{3}{2a}\,\frac{L^{2/3}-(\beta\eta)^{2/3}}{\varepsilon^{1/3}}=C_c\,\tau_\eta\left(\frac{Re_\lambda}{\sqrt{15}}-\beta^{2/3}\right),\qquad C_c=\frac{3}{2a},$$

using \(L/\eta=(Re_\lambda/\sqrt{15})^{3/2}\). The transit time is \(C_c\) large-eddy times \(u'^2/\varepsilon=\tfrac23k/\varepsilon\), less the part of the cascade below the tubes, and it vanishes at \(Re_\lambda=\sqrt{15}\,\beta^{2/3}\approx11\), where the tubes are the large eddies. The response of a tube itself, \(1/\gamma\approx5\,\tau_\eta\), is short compared with \(T_c\) above \(Re_\lambda\approx40\): the delay is that of the cascade, not of the formation of the tube. This is the idea of the multiple-time-scale models (Hanjalić et al. 1980; Schiestel 1987) and of the spectral relaxation model for scalars (Fox 1995), reduced here to the one lag the tube closure needs.

In a flow solver the lag is one transport equation for the dissipation rate that the tubes see, \(\varepsilon_t\),

$$\frac{D\varepsilon_t}{Dt}=\frac{\varepsilon-\varepsilon_t}{T_c}+\nabla\!\cdot\!\left(\frac{\nu_t}{\sigma}\nabla\varepsilon_t\right),$$

with \(\varepsilon\) the solver's dissipation rate, read as the rate at which energy enters the cascade, and the tube closure evaluated with \(\varepsilon_t\). In steady homogeneous turbulence \(\varepsilon_t=\varepsilon\) and the closure of the previous subsection is recovered. The constant \(C_c\) is of order one: halving the scale at each step gives 2.7, the observed lags correspond to 0.5 to 1 in units of the turnover time used by those authors. We propose \(C_c\) as the single constant to be calibrated, against the time series of injection and dissipation in forced simulations and against the yield of a fast competitive reaction at varying feed position in a stirred tank, where the lag moves the zone of intense micromixing downstream of the zone of intense energy input.

14. Limits and open questions

  • The swirl at high Reynolds number. Models I and II differ by a factor 1.68 at \(Re_\lambda=1000\). The all-tube law rests on Kida et al. (two simulations) and Mouri and Hori (one probe method, one fitted factor). A simulation above \(Re_\lambda\approx400\) analysed without a threshold would decide.
  • The second family of radii. The model's \(r_{\max}=5\eta\) is the first lognormal function of the radius distributions (mean 4.6 to 5.5 \(\eta\), 53 to 71% of the tubes). The second, broad function (median 8.5 to 16.8 \(\eta\)) is not in the model. The budget of section 7 varies as \(\beta^2\) and \(\beta^4\), so a closure of a property to which the larger structures contribute would need a second term for them. The radius divisor of the probe data (1.75) assumes that the probe average follows the first function.
  • Definitions. The core of Kida et al. is bounded by the inflection of the pressure, which for a Burgers vortex lies at \(0.66\,r_{\max}\); we follow the literature in comparing its diameter with the diameter of maximum swirl. Da Silva et al. give two inconsistent values of the swirl.
  • The budget. The volume fraction follows from assigning to the background the dissipation of a uniform strain at the rate of the tubes; it is checked against two measured values only.
  • The lag. The form of \(T_c\) is a scaling argument and \(C_c\) is not calibrated.
  • Range. Isotropic small scales, \(35\le Re_\lambda\le1934\); no wall or interface effects.

15. Conclusions

The vortex tubes of the dissipative range have a radius of maximum swirl of about \(5\eta\) (5.2 \(\eta\) fitted) in every flow examined, with only a very small reduction with the Reynolds number, from 5.3 \(\eta\) at \(Re_\lambda=100\) to 4.5 \(\eta\) at 2000; this is the firmest result. Their swirl is described by one law, \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=0.834\,Re_\lambda^{1/3}\), if probe data and the most intense tubes are corrected to a common level, and by two laws without swirl corrections if the most intense tubes and all tubes are taken as two populations. Model selection with leave-one-source-out validation shows that the data support no more than one or two parameters in either case. The Burgers budget then gives the strain rate, circulation, volume fraction and spacing of the tubes from \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\), which places the engulfment model of micromixing on measured ground, and a first-order lag with one constant accounts for the time the cascade takes to feed the tubes. The path of every number from its paper to the model is recorded and open to comment.

Appendix: the source data, how it was converted, and what the model uses

The appendix lists every source with its conversions, made from the same data file as the fits. Its paragraphs on the corrections (A0c) give the rationale as it was decided; the review of that rationale is in sections 9 and 12, and the page-by-page evidence is in the recording book (LIT/record).

Every literature value that enters or is compared with the model is listed here, source by source. For each paper there is a short discussion of how the tubes were selected and the equations that convert the tabulated numbers to the model quantities, followed by one table per measurement type, with the rows in ascending \(Re_\lambda\). Each table has the measurement type, \(Re_\lambda\), the kinematic viscosity \(\nu\) and the dissipation rate \(\varepsilon\) of the run (the two given quantities that fix \(\eta\) and \(u_\eta\); in the units of the paper, which differ: DNS code units, cm\(^2\)/s and m\(^2\)/s\(^3\); a dash where the paper does not give one), then the entries taken from the paper's table, then the value used in the model with the \(\nu\), \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\) used by the model in SI units, and the role: fitted in section 10, or not fitted with the reason. The model-side \(\nu\) and \(\varepsilon\) are measured for the laboratory experiments in air (Mouri et al.), derived from the Kolmogorov length for Aligolzadeh et al. (‡), and for all DNS rows a reference, water (\(\nu=10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)/s) at \(\varepsilon=0.1\) W/kg (†), explained in A0b. The tube set of each source (whole or intense) is explained in section 9.

A0. Conversions used for all sources

A Burgers vortex has \(u_\theta(r)=\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\left(1-e^{-r^2/R_B^2}\right)\) with \(R_B=2\sqrt{\nu/\gamma}\), the radius at which the vorticity has fallen to \(1/e\) of its axis value. The swirl is maximal at \(r_{\max}=\sqrt{x}\,R_B=1.121\,R_B\), where \(x=1.2564\) is the root of \(e^x-2x-1=0\), and

$$U_{\max}=\frac{(1-e^{-x})\,\Gamma}{2\pi\,r_{\max}},\qquad \frac{\Gamma}{\nu}=\frac{2\pi}{1-e^{-x}}\,\frac{r_{\max}U_{\max}}{\nu}=8.78\,Re_c,\qquad Re_c=\frac{r_{\max}U_{\max}}{\nu}.$$

The circulation inside a radius \(r\) is \(\Gamma(r)=\Gamma\left(1-e^{-r^2/R_B^2}\right)\) and the swirl at \(r=k\,r_{\max}\) is \(U_{\max}f(k)\), with

$$f(k)=\frac{1-e^{-xk^2}}{k\,(1-e^{-x})}.$$

The Kolmogorov scales satisfy \(\nu=u_\eta\,\eta\), and for isotropic turbulence the rms velocity is \(u'/u_\eta=\left(Re_\lambda/\sqrt{15}\right)^{1/2}\) (the isotropic relation \(\varepsilon=15\nu u'^2/\lambda^2\)). All radii are in units of \(\eta\), all velocities in units of \(u_\eta\) (written \(U_\eta\) in the model), and \(\Gamma\) in units of \(\nu\).

A0b. Physical equivalents of the DNS rows

A DNS is solved in dimensionless variables, \(\tilde x=x/\ell_0\), \(\tilde u=u/u_0\), \(\tilde t=t\,u_0/\ell_0\), \(\tilde\nu=\nu/(u_0\ell_0)\), \(\tilde\varepsilon=\varepsilon\,\ell_0/u_0^3\). Ghira et al. fix the box at \(2\pi\times2\pi\times2\pi\) (so \(\ell_0=L_{\text{box}}/2\pi\) and the Fourier wavenumbers are integers) and impose a random body force, delta-correlated in time and concentrated at the wavenumbers around \(k_p=2\) (Alvelius's scheme), whose mean power \(P=\langle f_iu_i\rangle=10\) is the same in every run. There are no walls and no mean flow; at steady state the viscous dissipation balances the power, so \(\tilde\varepsilon\approx10\) (Table II: 9.5–11.9) and the integral length \(\tilde L_{11}\approx0.85\) is set by the forcing. Only \(\tilde\nu\) changes between the runs (0.0145 to 0.0010), and it sets \(Re_\lambda\); the Kolmogorov length \(\tilde\eta=(\tilde\nu^3/\tilde\varepsilon)^{1/4}\) is the value listed in Table II (0.0235 for the first run). One series is therefore the same stirrer in fluids of falling viscosity.

To compare with a physical flow with kinematic viscosity \(\nu\) and dissipation rate \(\varepsilon\), the two scales \(\ell_0\) and \(u_0\) follow from two equations, \(\varepsilon=\tilde\varepsilon\,u_0^3/\ell_0\) and \(\nu=\tilde\nu\,u_0\ell_0\):

$$\ell_0=\frac{\eta_{\text{phys}}}{\tilde\eta}=\left(\frac{\nu^3/\varepsilon}{\tilde\nu^3/\tilde\varepsilon}\right)^{1/4},\qquad u_0=\frac{\nu}{\tilde\nu\,\ell_0},\qquad \eta_{\text{phys}}=\left(\frac{\nu^3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/4}.$$

The Reynolds number \(Re_\lambda\) is already used (through \(\tilde\nu\)), so one of \(\varepsilon\), \(\ell_0\) or \(u_0\) must be given besides \(\nu\). The model takes \(\varepsilon\) as given, as in section 7, and the reference used here is water, \(\nu=10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)/s, at \(\varepsilon=0.1\) W/kg, so \(\eta_{\text{phys}}=56.2\ \mu\)m. The results of the DNS in Kolmogorov units hold for any \(\varepsilon\); a different reference only rescales the lengths, and an \(r_{\max}\) of \(\beta\,\eta\) becomes \(\beta\times56.2\ \mu\)m. For the runs of Ghira et al. (2022), with the integral lengths of their Table II:

The column \(\tilde L_{11}\) is the DNS value (Ghira et al., Table II, in code units) and is given for information only: it is not converted to metres and is not used in the phenomenological turbulence model, whose inputs are \(\varepsilon\) and \(\nu\) (with \(\eta\) and the Kolmogorov scales following from them), and it enters none of the fits.

The tube Reynolds number and the circulation are recomputed from the corrected radius and swirl. The corrections are working choices, made to bring the experiments to the same tube as the simulations, and are listed with the reason for each:

The chord correction (hot wire, all tubes)

A single wire or crossed wire records one velocity component along a straight path through the flow. With Taylor's hypothesis the time is a distance \(s=Ut\), and a tube is a vortex with Gaussian vorticity \(\omega=\omega_0e^{-\rho^2/2R^2}\) (\(R\) its Gaussian width, \(R_B=\sqrt2\,R\), \(r_{\max}=\sqrt{2x}\,R=1.585\,R\)) and azimuthal velocity \(v_\theta=\omega_0R^2(1-e^{-\rho^2/2R^2})/\rho\). For a tube with axis \(\mathbf a\) crossed by a path with direction \(\mathbf e_x\) at impact parameter \(b\) (the distance between the path and the axis), the distance of the path from the axis is \(\rho^2=b^2+\sin^2\gamma\,(s-s_c)^2\), with \(\gamma\) the angle between path and axis, and the signal in the sensed direction \(\mathbf e_y\) is

$$S(s)=\frac{v_\theta(\rho)}{\rho}\;\mathbf e_y\cdot\left(\mathbf a\times\mathbf p(s)\right).$$

For a tube normal to the path and crossed through its axis the signal is \(v_\theta(|s|)\,\mathrm{sgn}\,s\): two extrema at \(\pm r_{\max}\), a spacing of \(2r_{\max}=3.17R\) (the rule \(R=0.31\,U\Delta t\) of Belin et al.) and an amplitude \(U_{\max}\). Off the axis the spacing grows and the amplitude falls (tube normal to the path):

\(b/r_{\max}\)00.511.523
spacing of the extrema \(/2r_{\max}\)1.001.041.201.532.003.00
amplitude \(/\) central amplitude1.000.890.660.460.350.23

A tilt of the axis stretches the path through the tube by \(1/\cos\alpha\) (mean 1.12 for a tilt uniform up to 45°, 1.41 at 45°) and adds an even part to the signal. Averaging over all orientations (isotropic, tilt up to 45°) and a uniform offset \(b\), keeping the events whose peak is at least a fraction \(f\) of the central amplitude (the detection threshold relative to the strength of the tube), averaging the profiles of the events that are kept (aligned on their zero crossing, as Mouri and Hori average the signals centred on each tube) and fitting a Burgers profile to the mean, as they do, the radius and the swirl of the fit relative to those of the tube are (tilt limit 45°, 1500 events for each cut; script fit_threshold.py):

amplitude cut \(f\)0.20.30.40.50.70.9
radius of the fit / true radius1.921.611.451.371.231.15
swirl of the fit / true swirl0.340.450.540.600.760.93
