A high threshold (large \(f\)) keeps only near-axis crossings (ratios close to 1); an average over all tubes includes weak crossings (small \(f\)). The radius ratio of 1.75 that brings the 8.8 \(\eta\) of Mouri and Hori (2009) to 5.0 \(\eta\) corresponds to \(f\approx0.25\) and a swirl ratio of 0.40, a swirl factor of 2.5. The tilt limit and the true radius move the factor between 1.7 and 3.9:

swirl factor needed (the radius ratio of the all-tube average)tilt limit 20°45°70°
true radius 4.97 \(\eta\) (ratio 1.67–1.85)2.8–3.32.4–2.82.0–2.4
true radius 4.5 \(\eta\) (ratio 1.84–2.05)3.2–3.92.7–3.42.4–2.9
true radius 5.4 \(\eta\) (ratio 1.53–1.71)2.4–2.92.0–2.51.7–2.1

The product \(Re_c'/Re_c\) of the fit is 0.7–0.8 at these cuts, so the mean-profile fit does not conserve the circulation. The factor 3 used is inside the range and puts the swirl on the common curve of section 10; 2.5 is also compatible with the data. Two limits of the model: it assumes identical tubes (the diameter pdf of the DNS of Tanahashi et al. has a core of width \(s=0.29\) in \(\ln D\) and a wide tail, section 9; the size distribution of Belin et al. needs \(s\approx0.5\) in the chord model, which the probe geometry does not separate from the true width), and it selects events by their peak signal, whereas Mouri's cut acts on the velocity increment over a short separation, which is a slope: for a separation of 0.5 \(R\) the ratios are 1.60 and 0.45 at \(f=0.1\) and 1.37 and 0.57 at \(f=0.2\), so a radius ratio of 1.75 needs \(f<0.1\), the whole distribution. Checks: (i) the size distribution that Belin et al. measured with a hot film has its peak at \(R=3.5\,\eta\) and its mean near \(6\,\eta\) (read from his Fig. 5); the peak is set by near-axis crossings and corresponds to \(r_{\max}=5.5\,\eta\), the mean divided by 1.7 gives \(5.6\,\eta\); the chord model fitted to the whole curve (fit_chord.py) gives a true radius of 3.8–4.2 \(\eta\) (\(r_{\max}\) 6–6.7 \(\eta\)) for a tilt limit of 0–45° and does not separate these limits; (ii) Mouri and Hori state that \(R_0\) is above the true mean radius for all tubes but close to it for intense tubes.

The probe has a finite length (1.25 mm sensing length and 1.4 mm wire separation for Mouri et al., against 0.2–3 \(\eta\) for the masked fibre of Belin et al.), which grows from 2 \(\eta\) at \(Re_\lambda=332\) to 13 \(\eta\) at 1934 and smooths the signal. A boxcar average over a length \(L\) adds \(L^2/6\) to \(R^2\) and conserves the circulation; for \(L=1\) mm and a true \(r_{\max}=5\,\eta\) it would give a radius of 5.1 \(\eta\) at \(Re_\lambda=332\) and 8.4 \(\eta\) at 1934. The hot-wire radii of Mouri et al. (2004, 2007) are below this estimate at high \(Re_\lambda\), and it is not applied. A fit of the chord model with the wire length added (fit_smoothing.py) to the threshold pairs and the all-tube values together does not settle the question: the wire length it needs is 2.9 mm against the real 1.0–1.25 mm, and with the real length it gives true radii of 2.7–3.7 \(\eta\), below every simulation, so it is not used.

Why the intense hot-wire classes are left out

The classes of Mouri et al. (2004, 2007) are the highest 0.1% and 1% of the absolute velocity increments of the same experiments as Mouri and Hori (2009); Fig. 2 of the latter shows that they are the tail of the distribution of the increments that the all-tube average also contains. The events above a high threshold are mostly crossings close to the axis, so their radii (5.2–7.4 \(\eta\)) are close to the true mean, as the authors write, and their swirl (4–14 \(U_\eta\)) is closer to the true swirl than that of the all-tube average. Two readings of the difference between the two values are possible: a chord distribution (the same tubes crossed at different offsets and tilts, as in Belin et al.) or a real difference in tube strength (the authors attribute the difference of V0 mainly to the true mean circulation velocity). The data cannot separate them. If it is the chord alone, the 0.1% row is a lower bound for the true swirl, which gives the all-tube swirl a factor of at least 3.1 at \(Re_\lambda=332\) and 4.4 at 1934; the factor 3 used is at the lower end of that bound. The tube that the chord model gives from the pair of rows depends on the tilt limit (swirl 10.9, 10.8 and 13.9 \(U_\eta\) at \(Re_\lambda=332\) for 20, 45 and 70°) and on whether the cut acts on the peak or on the increment (the ratio of the two cuts is 1.8 for the peak and 2.8 for the increment, against 1.86 read from the distribution of the increments in their Fig. 2), so the rows are not used as a calibration and are shown in A8 and A9 for comparison.

Ghira et al. (2022): the swirl

Their listed swirl \(U_{ivs}\), the mean tangential velocity at \(R_{ivs}\), is 1.0–1.25 \(u'\), against 0.86–0.99 for Jiménez and Wray, 0.68–0.76 for Da Silva et al., 0.5 for the mixing layer and 0.5–0.8 for the hot wire. The swirl that a Burgers vortex has with their mean axis vorticity (\(\omega_{ivs}/\omega_{rms}=3.9\), 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.8 at \(Re_\lambda=90\), 148, 191, 242, 314) and their Burgers radius is \(U_{\max}=0.319\,\omega_0R_B=5.5\), 5.9, 6.0, 6.0, 6.2 \(U_\eta\), nearly constant, while the listed swirl grows with \(u'\) from 6.1 to 9.5. The ratio of the vorticity-based to the listed swirl falls from 0.90 to 0.65. A constant factor that puts the Ghira swirl on the curve of the other sources, \(U_{\max}/U_\eta=0.79\,Re_\lambda^{0.34}\), is 0.58 (0.56–0.60 for the seven runs), and 0.6 was used; the derivation of section 9a, from the all-tube population of Pirozzoli (2012), gives 0.66–0.68, so 0.67 is used now, with a radius factor of 1.25. This is an empirical factor, closer to the vorticity argument at \(Re_\lambda\approx300\)–400 than at 90. More data at low \(Re_\lambda\) support moving Ghira et al. than the others: at \(Re_\lambda\) of 83–120 Kida et al. give 3.7–3.9 and Da Silva et al. 3.7–4.3, against 6.1–7.1 listed. With the Ghira swirl as listed no choice of the Mouri and Hori factor brings the fits below 17.5% (combined score), against 11.4% with the factors of section 9a.

A1. Ghira, Elsinga and da Silva (2022) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Table III (mean values for the intense vorticity structures, one row per simulation); Table II (\(\nu\) in code units); definitions in Sec. III, Eq. (8)–(10).

Method: DNS, forced isotropic

Which tubes: The structures are the points with the highest vorticity magnitude, 1% of the volume (the intense vorticity structures, IVS); the radius is where the azimuthal mean of the axial vorticity has fallen to \(1/e\) of its axis value.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=\sqrt{x}\,R_B=1.12\,\dfrac{R_{ivs}}{R_{ivs}/R_B}$$ $$\dfrac{\Gamma}{\nu}=\dfrac{2\pi}{K_B}\,Re_c=8.78\,\dfrac{r_{\max}}{\eta}\dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}\qquad(\text{total circulation from the converted radius and swirl; the listed }Re_\Gamma\text{ is not used})$$ $$\dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=\dfrac{U_{ivs}/u_\eta}{f(k)},\quad k=\dfrac{R_{ivs}/R_B}{\sqrt{x}},\quad f(k)=\dfrac{1-e^{-xk^2}}{k\,(1-e^{-x})}$$

Notes: Their \(\Gamma_{ivs}=2\pi\langle U_{ivs}\rangle R_{ivs}\) (Eq. 9) is the circulation inside \(R_{ivs}\), about 61% of the total of a Burgers vortex, and is about 0.83 of \(2\pi U_{ivs}R_{ivs}\) from the same table (162 against 136 at \(Re_\lambda=90\)), probably because the paper averages the product per structure. The total circulation is therefore taken from the converted radius and swirl, \(\Gamma/\nu=8.78\,Re_c\) with \(Re_c=(r_{\max}/\eta)(U_{\max}/U_\eta)\); the listed \(Re_\Gamma Re_\lambda^{-1/2}\) is kept in the table as the source value. The swirl row converts the swirl listed at \(R_{ivs}\) to the Burgers peak; the tubes are intense, so \(Re_c\) is about twice that of the whole tubes.

Correction applied: Radius multiplied by 1.25, swirl by 0.67. The criterion of Ghira et al. keeps the 1% of the volume with the strongest vorticity, a subset of the tubes that is smaller and faster than the whole population. Reference: Pirozzoli (2012), whose pdfs of the radius and of the maximum velocity are of all the vortex cores found, with no lower threshold on the vorticity; they are linked by his most frequent circulation, Γ/ν = 80, and the cut of Ghira et al. is applied to them with the tubes filling 35% of the flow (section 9a). The multipliers are the value of the reference over the value of the kept tubes: radius 1.22–1.28 (the narrow family of the radius pdf over the mean radius of the kept tubes), swirl 0.66–0.68 (all tubes over the kept tubes); 1.25 and 0.67 are used. Swirl: The listed \(U_{ivs}/u'=1.0\)–1.25 is high against the other simulations of intense tubes (Jiménez and Wray 0.86–0.99, Da Silva et al. 0.68–0.76, mixing layer 0.5) and the hot wire (0.5–0.8). Their own mean axis vorticity (\(\omega_{ivs}/\omega_{rms}=3.9\)–4.8, Table III) and the Burgers radius imply a peak swirl of 5.5–6.2 \(U_\eta\) at all \(Re_\lambda\), against the listed 6–9.5: the excess grows with \(u'\), which suggests that the swirl at \(R_{ivs}\) includes a velocity from the surrounding flow. A constant factor of 0.58 (0.56–0.60 for the seven runs) puts the swirl on the curve \(U_{\max}/U_\eta\propto Re_\lambda^{0.34}\) of the other sources; 0.6 was used before the derivation from the population, which gives 0.66–0.68. At the same \(Re_\lambda\) of 83–120 the swirl of Kida et al. (3.7–3.9) and Da Silva et al. (3.7–4.3) is well below the listed 6.1–7.1, so more data at low \(Re_\lambda\) support moving Ghira et al. than moving the others; with the swirl as listed the fits are 17–19% off, against 8% with the factor. See A0c.

A2. Ghira, Elsinga and da Silva (2025) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Table 2 (characteristics of the IVS of all simulations, obtained as in the 2022 paper: \(R_{ivs}/\eta\) and \(U_{ivs}/u'\)); Table 1 of the same paper for \(\nu\) and \(\varepsilon\).

Method: DNS, forced isotropic

Which tubes: As Ghira et al. (2022): the intense vorticity structures, 1% of the volume.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=1.12\,\dfrac{R_{ivs}}{R_{ivs}/R_B},\qquad R_{ivs}/R_B=0.97\ (\text{assumed})$$

Notes: Only the two \(Re_\lambda=54\) radii are new: the other rows of Table 2 (4.28, 4.23, 4.10, 4.06 at \(Re_\lambda=91\), 143, 189, 239) are the simulations of the 2022 paper. Table 2 gives no \(R_{ivs}/R_B\) for these runs (Table 11 gives 0.99 and 0.97 for a repeated \(512^3\) run), so the mean of the 2022 values, 0.97, is assumed. The paper gives no circulation.

Correction applied: The same method and group as Ghira et al. (2022) (the 1% of the volume with the strongest vorticity): the same factors, radius 1.25 and swirl 0.67, so that the two papers are treated alike (see the correction of Ghira et al. 2022). See A0c.

A3. Jiménez, Wray, Saffman and Rogallo (1993) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Table 3 (average worm characteristics from the tracking algorithm, one row per simulation); the algorithm is described in the text above the table.

Method: DNS, forced isotropic

Which tubes: Worms: connected regions of vorticity above a threshold (the 1% of the volume of highest vorticity); the radius is the \(1/e\) radius of a Gaussian fitted to the azimuthal mean of the axial vorticity.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=\sqrt{x}\,R_B=1.12\,R$$ $$\dfrac{\Gamma}{\nu}=\dfrac{Re_\gamma}{Re_\lambda^{1/2}}\,Re_\lambda^{1/2}$$ $$\dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=\dfrac{\Gamma/\nu}{8.784\,r_{\max}/\eta}\qquad(\text{the swirl is not listed: derived from the total circulation and the radius})$$

Notes: The \(1/e\) radius of a Gaussian vorticity profile is the Burgers radius. The circulation of the table is that of the fitted Gaussian (the total circulation): \(\Gamma/\nu=Re_\gamma\). \(\nu\) is not read here because the copy of Table 1 is a scan.

A4. Tanahashi, Iwase and Miyauchi (2001) (whole tubes)

Where in the paper: Fig. 7 and the text around it (DNS of a turbulent mixing layer, \(Re_{\theta0}=500\)).

Method: DNS, mixing layer

Which tubes: Coherent fine-scale eddies educed from the local maxima of the second invariant of the velocity gradient (the scheme of Tanahashi et al. 1999; the statistics are those of every eddy found, thresholds are used for visualisation only: Q* >= 0.03 and Q* Re_lambda >= 1); the radius is the distance from the centre to the maximum of the mean azimuthal velocity.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=\dfrac{D}{2}$$

Notes: The probability density function of the diameter peaks at \(D\approx9\,\eta\) (the text says the mean diameter stays about \(8\,\eta\)). Fig. 1(b) of the paper gives \(Re_\lambda\) against time: about 80 (75–85, read from the figure) for \(Re_{\omega,0}=500\) at the times analysed (\(t=70\)–130); the text says the highest value is about 100, for \(Re_{\omega,0}=900\). Ghira et al. (2022), Table I, list this flow at \(Re_\lambda=80\)–100. (Until 2026-11-12 the page assumed 200.)

A5. Aligolzadeh, Holzner and Dawson (2023) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Sec. 2 (the von Kármán facility; DNS of Li et al. at \(Re_\lambda=418\)); Sec. 3.1 and the Conclusions (the mean radius); Fig. 12 and the text before it (the ratio \(R/R_B\)).

Method: 3D scanning PIV, water tank

Which tubes: Objectively defined vortices (Haller et al.) detected in 3D PIV data (resolution about \(1\,\eta\)); they occupy 1.4% of the volume. \(R\) is the distance from the axis to the boundary of the vortex, and \(R_B=(4\nu/\gamma_0)^{1/2}\) comes from the centre-line stretching rate (their Eq. 2.5).

Conversion: $$R_B=\dfrac{R}{R/R_B},\qquad r_{\max}=\sqrt{x}\,R_B=1.12\,\dfrac{R}{R/R_B}$$

Notes: Assumptions: the value 5.1 and the mean \(R/R_B=0.95\) are those of the experiment (the text gives the two means as 0.95 and 1.1, and says the experimental pdf is skewed to the left of 1). The DNS mean \(R/R_B=1.1\) cannot be used because the paper gives no separate DNS radius. The radius is larger than those of the DNS studies.

A6. Da Silva, Dos Reis and Pereira (2011) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Sec. 3 (the text before and after Table 1 and Fig. 3): forced isotropic turbulence (HIT) at \(Re_\lambda=111\) and the turbulent plane jet at \(Re_\lambda=120\) (deep inside the shear layer).

Method: DNS, isotropic and plane jet

Which tubes: Intense vorticity structures as in Ghira et al. (1% of the volume); \(R\) is the \(1/e\) radius of the vorticity, \(u_0\) the mean tangential velocity at \(R\), \(R_B\) the Burgers radius from the stretching rate.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=1.12\,\dfrac{R}{R/R_B}$$ $$\dfrac{U_{ivs}}{u_\eta}=\dfrac{u_0}{u'}\left(\dfrac{Re_\lambda}{\sqrt{15}}\right)^{1/2},\qquad \dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=\dfrac{U_{ivs}/u_\eta}{f(k)}$$

Notes: Conflict in the paper (found on the page image 2026-11-12): Table 1 prints \(\langle u_0\rangle/u_\eta=9.0\) (HIT) and 7.15 (jet), and its \(Re_\Gamma Re_\lambda^{-1/2}=28.8\) and 28.3 with \(\Gamma=2\pi Ru_0\) give \(u_0/u_\eta=10.5\) and 10.7; the values used here, 3.6 and 4.2, come from \(u_0/u'\) times \(u'/u_\eta=(Re_\lambda/\sqrt{15})^{1/2}\). The two differ by a factor 2.5, so the swirl of this source is left out of the fits. The text gives \(R/\eta=4.6\) for both flows, \(u_0/u'=0.68\) and 0.76, and \(R/R_B=0.99\) and 0.97. Table 1 of the paper (a compilation of IVS data from the literature) is an image and was not read, and the circulation Reynolds number quoted there uses a different definition (\(Re_\Gamma Re_\lambda^{-1/2}\approx28\)), so it is not used. Their \(u_0/u'\) (0.7–0.8) is lower than that of Ghira et al. (1.0–1.25).

A7. Mouri and Hori (2009) (whole tubes)

Where in the paper: Table 2 (parameters of vortex tubes in boundary layers B1–B6 and duct flows D1–D5), \(Re_\lambda\) from Table 1 of the same paper; \(\nu\) from Table I of Mouri et al. (2007) for the same experiments. Published as Fluid Dyn. Res. 41, 021402 (the file is the preprint).

Method: hot wire, 1D velocity increments

Which tubes: All vortex tubes: the conditionally averaged spanwise velocity around moderate enhancements of the velocity increment is fitted with a Burgers profile; \(R_0\) and \(V_0\) are the radius and the maximum circulation velocity of the fit.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=R_0,\qquad \dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=\dfrac{V_0}{u_K},\qquad Re_c=Re_0=\dfrac{R_0V_0}{\nu}$$

Notes: The authors say \(R_0\) is larger and \(V_0\) smaller than the true means, because off-centre and inclined tubes are included. The radius and the swirl are corrected (A0c: radius divided by 1.75, swirl multiplied by 3) and both are fitted; the listed \(Re_0\) is not fitted, the tube Reynolds number follows from the corrected values.

Correction applied: Radius divided by 1.75 and swirl multiplied by 3. The authors fit the mean profile of all tubes: the tube positions are all the local extrema of the Gaussian-smoothed velocity increment (scale about \(6\,\eta\)), so weak and off-axis crossings count as much as central ones. A hot-wire path crosses a tube at a random offset from its axis and a random tilt, and the radius read is the spacing of the two extrema of the signal, which grows with the offset, so the radius is too large and, for the same crossings, the amplitude too small. Mouri and Hori say that \(R_0\) is greater than the true mean radius and \(V_0\) less than the true mean circulation velocity for all vortex tubes, because of tubes with \(|y_0|\gtrsim R_0\) and \(\theta_0\ne0\). Radius: the chord model (A0c, tilt limit 45°) gives a ratio of 1.75 for the mean profile of an all-tube average (an amplitude cut of about a quarter of the central swirl), so the true radius is \(8.8/1.75=5.0\,\eta\), the value of the other sources. Swirl: the same crossings lower the amplitude by a factor 2–3.5 (tilt limit 20–70°, true radius 4.5–5.4 \(\eta\)); the factor 3 is the value at which the swirl lies within 3% of the common curve through Ghira et al. (×0.6), Da Silva et al. and Kida et al. (the data allow 2.5 as well). The threshold averages of Mouri et al. (2004, 2007) come from the same experiments and are left out of the fits (A8, A9). See A0c.

A8. Mouri, Hori and Kawashima (2007) (intense tubes)

Which tubes: Intense vortical structures: the highest 0.1% or 1% of the absolute spanwise-velocity increments; the averaged profile is fitted with a Burgers vortex. A9. Mouri, Hori and Kawashima (2004) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Table I (experimental conditions, flow characteristics and parameters of vortex tubes; one column per data set; boundary layers, \(Re_\lambda=295\)–1258).

Method: hot wire, 1D velocity increments

Which tubes: The highest 1% of the absolute spanwise-velocity increments (intense tubes), fitted with a Burgers profile.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=R_0,\qquad \dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=\dfrac{V_0}{u_K},\qquad Re_c=Re_0=\dfrac{R_0V_0}{\nu}$$

Notes: The table is a scrambled text layer; the six data sets were read in order of \(Re_\lambda\). \(V_0\) is about half the r.m.s. velocity (0.46–0.60) and \(Re_0\propto Re_\lambda^{1/2}\); these values agree with Mouri et al. (2007) at 1% threshold.

A11. Belin, Maurer, Tabeling and Willaime (1996) (intense tubes)

Where in the paper: Sec. 4 (Burgers filament crossing the probe, Eqs. (6)–(8)); Sec. 5 and Fig. 5 (size distributions of the worms for \(Re_\lambda=151\)–718, mean size \(R=3.5\,\eta\)); Sec. 7 (\(Re_\lambda>700\)).

Method: hot film, 1D velocity derivative, helium

Which tubes: Intense events in the tails of the pdf of the velocity derivative, in helium gas between counter-rotating disks (hot film on a 7 \(\mu\)m carbon fibre, resolution 0.2–3 \(\eta\)), selected by conditional sampling and interpreted as Burgers filaments crossing the probe close to their axis; \(R\) is the Gaussian width of the vorticity, \(\omega=\omega_0e^{-r^2/2R^2}\).

Conversion: $$R=0.31\,U\,\Delta t\quad(\text{peak spacing }\Delta x=U\Delta t\approx3.2\,R=2\,r_{\max})$$ $$r_{\max}=\sqrt{2x}\,R=1.585\,R\qquad(R_B=\sqrt{2}\,R)$$

Notes: The method measures a time record, which the mean velocity \(U\) turns into a distance (frozen flow); the radius follows from the spacing of the two extrema of the signal as the filament passes, and the peak amplitude gives \(U_{\max}\). The value \(R=3.5\,\eta\) is the position of the maximum of the size distribution seen by the probe (Fig. 5, which collapses for \(Re_\lambda=151\)–718), quoted by the authors as the mean worm size; the same distribution built from the DNS of Jiménez et al. through the same probe geometry (their Eq. 9) peaks at 2.8 \(\eta\), so the probe sizes are 1.25 times the DNS sizes. The distribution is skewed with a tail to about 20 \(\eta\), and a rough reading of the figure puts its mean near 6 \(\eta\) and its median near 5 \(\eta\). The row uses the median of the digitised Fig. 5, \(r_{\max}=1.585\times4.8=7.6\,\eta\) (the peak, 5.5 \(\eta\), is a statistic of the chord distribution), as a range of \(Re_\lambda\); the wire-and-tube model corrects it (appendix A0c). Above \(Re_\lambda\approx700\) the size distribution widens: the mean velocity increment across the filament decreases and its mean radius increases so that the circulation does not change; the authors read this as an instability of the filaments. The paper has no table of \(R\), \(U_{\max}\) or the circulation by \(Re_\lambda\).

Meas. type\(Re_\lambda\)\(\nu\)\(\varepsilon\)\(R/\eta\)ModelRole

range

A12. Kida, Goto and Makihara (2002) (whole tubes)

Where in the paper: Table 2 (a table image; characteristic quantities of the low-pressure vortices at the two resolutions) and Table 1 (\(Re_\lambda\), \(\nu\) in code units); the core boundary is shown in Fig. 3(a).

Method: DNS, forced isotropic

Which tubes: Low-pressure vortices: the cores occupy 31–35% of the volume; \(D\) is the diameter of the (non-circular) core boundary, \(u_\theta\) the mean azimuthal velocity at the boundary, \(\Gamma\) the circulation along it.

Conversion: $$r_{\max}=\dfrac{D}{2},\qquad \dfrac{\Gamma}{\nu}\ \text{as listed (inside the boundary)}$$ $$\dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=1.175\,\dfrac{u_\theta}{u_K}\ (\text{boundary taken at }0.6\,r_{\max}\text{, where }f=0.855)$$ $$\dfrac{d}{\eta}=\dfrac{D}{2\eta}\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{V_{\text{core}}/V}}\qquad(L_e=\dfrac{V_{\text{core}}/V}{\pi(D/2)^2},\ d=L_e^{-1/2})$$

Notes: The factor 1.175 assumes that the boundary encloses 60% of the enstrophy of a Burgers vortex, which puts it at \(0.6\,r_{\max}\); then \(f(0.6)=0.855\). This is an assumption of mine, and the boundary radius is not the Burgers peak radius.

A13. Pirozzoli (2009, 2012) (whole tubes)

Method: DNS, isotropic

Which tubes: Vortex cores scanned out of the DNS database without a vorticity threshold (candidate centres at local maxima of the vorticity modulus in the coordinate planes, vorticity within 20 degrees of the plane normal, a clear swirling pattern required; \(r_0\) the radius of maximum velocity); all classes of vortices.

Papers read for which no row was used

Ghira et al. (2024) has the \(Re_\lambda=54\) DNS but no radius or swirl for it (its radius is that of Ghira et al. 2025, Table 2). Elsinga et al. (2023) has the enstrophy and dissipation scaling to \(Re_\lambda=1445\), with a change near \(Re_\lambda\approx250\) where large-scale shear layers develop, and no tube dimensions. Watanabe and Nagata (2023) and Watanabe et al. (2024) describe shear layers (half-width \(\ell_S/\eta\approx4\), velocity jump \(\Delta u_S/u_\eta\approx5\) at \(Re_\lambda\) 43–202; aspect ratio about 4.5 at \(Re_\lambda\) 400–900), not tubes. Enoki et al. (2023) give the r.m.s. shares of the shear and non-shear velocities (70% and 30%). Leung et al. (2012) analyse the geometry of educed structures at \(Re_\lambda=141\) without a tube radius. Okamoto et al. (2007) extract coherent vortices at \(Re_\lambda\) 167–732 by wavelets and report degrees of freedom, not a radius. Cherry and Kwon (1990) take a Burgers vortex as the Kolmogorov eddy, with strain \(0.18\,(\varepsilon/\nu)^{1/2}\) for stirred vessels, \(r_{\max}=2\sqrt{1.265\,\nu/\alpha}=5.3\,\eta\) (computed here), \(\omega_0=7.14\,(\varepsilon/\nu)^{1/2}\) and a half-spacing of \(20\,\eta\); this is a model eddy without a stated \(Re_\lambda\), and the half-spacing is close to the model \(d/\eta\) of 17–19 at \(Re_\lambda\) 170–330. Wojtas et al. (2017) has no tube data.

Appendix: the fitting measure of Fig. 1b (a weighted sum of squares)

Written so that the fits of section 9 can be repeated: the formula, where it comes from, how its one factor is derived, and the values it takes for the data of Fig. 1b.

B1. Definition

A model \(c_i=f(Re_{\lambda,i};\theta)\) with \(p\) fitted parameters \(\theta\) is fitted to \(N\) values \(e_i\) (the experimental or simulated values of \(r_{\max}/\eta\) or of \(U_{\max}/U_\eta\), after the corrections). The fit minimises the corrected sum of relative error $$S=b\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{c_i}{e_i}\right)^2+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{(c_i-e_i)^2}{\bar e^{\,2}},\qquad \bar e=\frac1N\sum_i e_i,$$ and its quality is reported as the standard error of the fit, dimensionless, $$s=\sqrt{\frac{S}{N-p}} .$$ The first sum is the relative error of each point and the second the absolute error, in units of the mean of the data, of each point; \(b\) is a factor derived in B3. Every point has the same weight, whatever its source; there is no weight per source.

B2. Where it comes from

Two measures are in common use. The sum of the squared relative errors, \(\sum(1-c/e)^2=\sum(c-e)^2/e^2\), divides each misfit by \(e^2\): a misfit of 10% counts the same at \(e=2\) and at \(e=16\), but in the fit the points of small \(e\) have a large weight and those of large \(e\) hardly count. The sum of the squared absolute errors, \(\sum(c-e)^2\), does the reverse: the absolute scatter of the data grows with their size, so the large values dominate the misfit and the small values are ignored. The data of Fig. 1b span a factor of ten in the swirl (1.6 to 17.2) and scatter widely from source to source, so neither measure alone is acceptable.

The author has used this weighted sum of squares in earlier work to balance the contribution of the small and of the large values without one of them dominating. That matters in particular when data with a significant spread are fitted, as is the case here. It is not a published standard measure; in effect it resembles the combined error model, in which the variance of a point has a constant part and a part proportional to its value, but its factor \(b\) is fixed from the data by the condition below and not fitted.

B3. The factor b

Since \((1-c/e)^2=(c-e)^2/e^2\), the sum is a weighted least squares, $$S=\sum_i (c_i-e_i)^2\,w(e_i),\qquad w(e)=\frac{b}{e^2}+\frac{1}{\bar e^{\,2}} .$$ The second part of the weight is the same for every point. The first part, \(b/e^2\), is the relative error: at the mean, \(1/\bar e^{\,2}\), it equals the weight of the absolute error (for \(b=1\)), above it for the values below the mean and below it for the values above. For a given \(b\) the relative part is balanced between the two ends of the data when its deficit at the largest value equals \(b\) times its excess at the smallest, the points being spread evenly through the decades so that the two extremes stand for the whole range: $$-\left(\frac{1}{e_{\max}^2}-\frac{1}{\bar e^{\,2}}\right)=b\left(\frac{1}{e_{\min}^2}-\frac{1}{\bar e^{\,2}}\right).$$ Solving for \(b\) and multiplying numerator and denominator by \(\bar e^{\,2}\), $$b=\frac{\dfrac{1}{\bar e^{\,2}}-\dfrac{1}{e_{\max}^2}}{\dfrac{1}{e_{\min}^2}-\dfrac{1}{\bar e^{\,2}}}=\frac{1-\bar e^{\,2}/e_{\max}^2}{\bar e^{\,2}/e_{\min}^2-1},$$ which is positive, since \(e_{\min}\lt\bar e\lt e_{\max}\), and is computed for each fit from the values that enter it. For \(b\to0\) the measure is the absolute error and the weights of all points are equal; for \(b=1\) it is the plain sum of the relative and the absolute error. The ratio of the weight of the smallest value to that of the largest is $$\frac{w(e_{\min})}{w(e_{\max})}=\frac{b/e_{\min}^2+1/\bar e^{\,2}}{b/e_{\max}^2+1/\bar e^{\,2}} .$$

B4. Values for Fig. 1b

For the radius (50 values from 4.0 to 6.2, mean 5.1) \(b=0.52\) and the weight ratio is 1.4 to 1; for the swirl (50 values from 1.6 to 17.2, mean 8.5) \(b=0.028\) and the ratio is 1.8 to 1 (all values without the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori; with it \(b=0.66\) for the radius and \(0.027\) for the swirl). With \(b=1\) the swirl would have a ratio of 23 to 1 and be fitted mostly at its small values. The models fitted are, for the radius, a constant, a power law and a straight line, and for the swirl a power law with a free exponent, the exponents 1/3 and 1/2, and a straight line; \(p\) is 1 for a constant and a fixed exponent and 2 otherwise, and the model of the lowest \(s\) is taken. Without the all-tube average of Mouri and Hori the lowest \(s\) is 0.117 for the radius (a straight line) and 0.134 for the swirl (the free power law, whose exponent is 0.47; the exponent 1/2 has 0.134).
